articles.title_original: Single‐Photon Emitters in Thickness‐Controlled hBN Directly Grown on Silicon Platform
articles.title_en: Transfer-Free hBN Growth on Silicon Enables Integrated Single-Photon Sources
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has emerged as a leading host for room‐temperature quantum light emission in 2D platforms, which enables facile integration with various photonic devices. However, scalable hBN growth is often restricted to ultrathin films and limited substrate choices, making transfer steps necessary for practical device integration. Here, we report catalyst‐free chemical vapor deposition of thickness‐controlled hBN films directly on CMOS‐compatible SiO 2 /Si substrates, enabling transfer‐free, large‐area growth of hBN hosting single‐photon emitters (SPEs). By systematically tuning the growth parameters, we engineered the SPE density from 2 × 10 7 to 7 × 10 7 cm −2 , and identified the optimal growth condition to yield the highest emitter density. Photophysical measurements confirm high‐purity emission with g 2 (0) down to 0.09 without background correction. Importantly, SPEs are well‐isolated in substantially thick hBN layers up to 100 nm, providing a device‐relevant thickness regime for optical mode confinement and fabrication of integrated photonic architectures. These results provide a scalable route to integrate hBN‐hosted quantum light sources on silicon platforms for large‐area quantum photonic devices.

articles.title_en: 3D Boron Nitride Framework Improves Epoxy Thermal Conductivity at Low Loading
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The ongoing miniaturization and integration of third‐generation wide‐bandgap semiconductor devices demand advanced thermal management packaging materials. Traditional polymer composites often rely on high filler loadings due to a lack of structured three‐dimensional (3D) networks, resulting in limited thermal improvement and deteriorated dielectric properties. In this study, a gelation–drying strategy was used to fabricate four distinct, continuous three‐dimensional thermal conduction networks within an epoxy resin (EP) matrix. The four networks were constructed using boron nitride (BN) platelets of different sizes (0.2, 2, 5, and 25 μm, respectively). It is demonstrated that the synergy between large‐scale BN fillers and the 3D scaffold enables the establishment of continuous phonon‐matched heat conduction pathways at a low percolation threshold, thereby substantially elevating the thermal conductivity of the EP composites. Benefiting from this unique architecture, the 25 μm 3D‐BN/EP composite achieves an out‐of‐plane thermal conductivity of 0.95 W/(m K) at a low loading of only 10 wt%. This value is 131.7% higher than that of the randomly blended BN/EP, yielding a high thermal conductivity enhancement efficiency of 42.78%. Simultaneously, the composite maintained excellent dielectric performance ( ɛ r = 3.82, tan δ = 0.0172 at 10 6 Hz and 25°C) and good insulation. This BN particle‐size‐regulated 3D network strategy provides a new method for the design of next‐generation epoxy composites for high‐power electronic packaging applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed continuous 3D boron nitride networks in epoxy, achieving 0.95 W/(m·K) out-of-plane thermal conductivity at 10 wt% loading. The approach also preserved dielectric performance, supporting potential use in high-power semiconductor packaging.

articles.title_original: Unveiling Graphitic Carbon Nitride in Hexagonal Boron Nitride Epitaxy on Sapphire
articles.title_en: Graphitic Carbon Nitride Enables Epitaxial hBN Growth on Sapphire
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Epitaxial growth of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) on sapphire is of fundamental importance for the development of van der Waals heterostructures, yet the mechanism of crystallographic alignment across a weakly bonded interface remains unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that graphitic carbon nitride (g‐C 3 N 4 ), unintentionally formed during Metal–Organic Vapor Phase Epitaxy (MOVPE) from triethylboron and ammonia precursors, plays a pivotal role in transferring lattice orientation from the Al 2 O 3 substrate to the overgrown hBN film. High‐resolution transmission electron microscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, X‐ray diffraction, photoluminescence, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy consistently reveal a nanometer‐thick interfacial region composed of AlN:O and g‐C 3 N 4 . Despite its partial amorphization upon post‐growth cooling, the layered structure of g‐C 3 N 4 provides the necessary structural flexibility to accommodate lattice mismatch and transmit crystallographic information across the interface. This finding establishes g‐C 3 N 4 as an effective buffer enabling epitaxial growth of two‐dimensional hBN on a three‐dimensional substrate. These insights suggest that the presence of carbon at the growth interface, often regarded as detrimental, can in fact be critical for achieving wafer‐scale, high‐quality epitaxial hBN, opening new directions for interface engineering in 2D material synthesis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that an interfacial layer of graphitic carbon nitride and AlN:O transfers lattice orientation from sapphire to epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride during MOVPE. The finding could support wafer-scale hBN synthesis and improved 2D-material interface engineering.

articles.title_original: Dual‐Input Two‐Dimensional Floating‐Gate Memory With Intrinsic Stochasticity for Secure Information Processing
articles.title_en: Graphene Floating-Gate Memory Enables Stochastic Hardware Encryption
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT 2D materials have enabled diverse electronic and optoelectronic devices, yet intrinsic stochastic behaviors are commonly regarded as detrimental to device reliability and controllability. Here, we demonstrate a dual‐input 2D floating‐gate memory that deliberately harnesses intrinsic stochastic optoelectronic responses as a functional degree of freedom for secure information processing. By integrating electrical gating and optical excitation within a Bi 2 O 2 S/h‐BN/graphene heterostructure, the floating‐gate device simultaneously achieves non‐volatility, multilevel programmability, and reconfigurable device‐intrinsic stochastic conductance responses. The memory exhibits a high on/off current ratio (>10 6 ), a wide memory window (83.4%), long retention (10 4 s), and robust endurance (>2000 cycles), enabling stable hardware‐level extraction of physical features. As a representative application, the stochastic optoelectronic features are combined with standard cryptographic primitives to realize reversible text and image encryption with pronounced diffusion and avalanche characteristics, while session‐level freshness is naturally supported to mitigate replay attacks and key reuse. Beyond cryptography, this work establishes a materials‐enabled strategy for transforming intrinsic stochasticity in 2D floating‐gate devices from an undesired effect into a useful functionality, opening new opportunities for multifunctional memory and secure information processing architectures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a dual-input floating-gate memory using a Bi₂O₂S/h-BN/graphene heterostructure, combining nonvolatile multilevel operation with intrinsic stochastic conductance. The device supports hardware-level feature extraction and reversible text and image encryption, positioning stochastic 2D memory for secure information-processing architectures.

articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene–Graphene Materials for Flexible Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract: Supercapacitors are promising electrochemical energy-storage devices known for high power density, rapid charge–discharge rates, long cycle life, and good mechanical flexibility. Their performance depends strongly on the properties of electrode and electrolyte materials, as well as factors such as ion transport and operating voltage. In recent years, two-dimensional materials, particularly MXenes, have gained significant attention for flexible supercapacitor applications. Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene offers high electrical conductivity, hydrophilic surfaces, layered structure, and favourable electrochemical properties, making it a suitable electrode material. Graphene and other carbon-based materials can further enhance conductivity and structural stability when combined with MXene. This review examines the role of MXene-based electrodes and different electrolyte systems in improving capacitance, energy density, power density, and cycling stability. It also discusses major challenges, including MXene restacking, oxidation, limited ion accessibility, and the development of flexible gel and solid-state electrolytes. The combination of MXene electrodes with suitable electrolytes provides considerable potential for lightweight, flexible, and efficient energy-storage devices.
articles.summary_en: The review evaluates MXene electrodes, graphene additives, and flexible gel or solid-state electrolytes for improving supercapacitor capacitance, energy density, power density, and cycling stability. It identifies MXene restacking, oxidation, limited ion accessibility, and electrolyte development as key challenges.

articles.title_original: Hexagonal Boron Nitride Nanosheets via Salt‐Assisted Strategies
articles.title_en: Salt-Assisted Strategies Advance Scalable Hexagonal Boron Nitride Nanosheet Production
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) hexagonal boron nitride nanosheets (h‐BNNSs) are versatile platforms for thermal, mechanical, and catalytic applications. However, scalable preparation that preserves both structural integrity and economic feasibility is still a major bottleneck. Herein, we review the progress in the versatility of salt‐assisted preparation and modification of h‐BNNS, where ionic compounds enable a controllable physicochemical environment for material engineering. In bottom‐up synthesis, the molten salt medium enhances mass transfer and lowers reaction barriers, promoting controlled crystal growth. In top‐down exfoliation, ion intercalation overcomes the interlayer van der Waals force to enable efficient production of high‐quality nanosheets. Meanwhile, the chemically active ionic environment bridges preparation and modification, allowing elemental doping, interface engineering, and nanoparticle loading to tailor properties and expand applications. Finally, we summarize key bottlenecks and outline future directions toward scalable, controllable, and application‐oriented salt‐assisted h‐BNNS engineering.
articles.summary_en: A review examines molten-salt synthesis and ion-assisted exfoliation routes for producing high-quality hexagonal boron nitride nanosheets. Salt environments can also support doping, interface engineering, and nanoparticle loading, but scalability and process control remain key challenges.

articles.title_original: A First-Principles Field Theory of Fluctuation Phenomena and Dielectric Screening in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures: Keldysh-Rytova Potentials, Moiré Superlattice Corrugations, and Coherent Transport Limits
articles.title_en: First-Principles Model of Noise and Screening in 2D Graphene Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors—such as monolayer MoS2, WS2, graphene, and transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures—represent rigorous testbeds for condensed-matter transport. Because the entire electronic channel is confined to an atomic sheet (), the absence of bulk dielectric screening leaves carriers highly exposed to substrate impurities, interfacial traps, and moiré potential modulations. Traditional noise models rely on empirical fitting parameters that fail to capture dielectric environment-dependent screening and lattice corrugations. Here, we present a first-principles field theory of fluctuation phenomena in 2D van der Waals channels by reformulating transport across a continuous inter-site electrostatic potential manifold. Incorporating the Keldysh-Rytova non-local potential kernel proves that effective energetic disorder narrows inversely with environmental dielectric permittivity (). In atomically abrupt heterostructures where correlation lengths exceed hopping distances (), transport shifts to the coherent domain limit, replacing random point-defect scattering with deterministic moiré superlattice potentials and yielding unprecedented suppression of low-frequency excess noise (exceeding six orders of magnitude in the effective Hooge parameter). In this work, Operando Differential Noise Spectroscopy (DJS) fingerprints and companion MATLAB simulation toolboxes confirm the emergence of discrete, symmetry-protected mini-band satellite resonances, providing a robust design framework for ultra-clean 2D quantum devices, low-noise cryogenic amplifiers, and multi-millisecond quantum coherent hardware.
articles.summary_en: The study presents a theoretical framework for dielectric screening, disorder and coherent transport in two-dimensional van der Waals channels including graphene. It reports simulated and spectroscopy-supported predictions of suppressed low-frequency noise and moiré miniband resonances, with potential relevance to quantum and low-noise electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Critical temperatures and collapsing of two-dimensional Log gases
articles.title_en: Study Characterizes Critical Collapse in Two-Dimensional Log Gases
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We consider the canonical ensemble of a system of point particles on the sphere interacting via a logarithmic pair potential. We study the behavior of the associated Gibbs measure as the inverse temperature approaches a critical value at which the partition function diverges. One of our main results shows that the Gibbs measure converges weakly to a probability measure supported on degenerate configurations in which certain subsets of particles collapse. We characterize the possible clusters in the limiting configurations in terms of the solutions of a discrete optimization problem, which also determines the critical inverse temperature. Our approach relies on the Fulton–MacPherson compactification of configuration spaces and meromorphic continuation of complex powers. For the two-component plasma with arbitrary charges, we solve the optimization problem explicitly and thereby obtain a complete description of the possible limiting clusters. In particular, the limiting measure is supported on configurations where a maximal number of positive–negative dipoles have formed. Allowing completely general charges is motivated in part by Onsager’s model of turbulence. In this context, we establish explicit probabilistic bounds for the critical inverse temperature in case of random coupling and charges, using general estimates expressed in terms of eigenvalues of the coupling matrix.
articles.summary_en: Researchers analyze how two-dimensional logarithmic particle systems behave near critical temperature, where the Gibbs measure collapses onto degenerate configurations. The work identifies limiting cluster structures, including positive–negative dipole formation in two-component plasmas, and derives bounds for random couplings and charges.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Derived Hybrid Micro/Nanofibers for Environmental Remediation
articles.title_en: Review Examines Graphene-Derived Fibers for Environmental Remediation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The potential health risks that industrial pollutants pose to humans and aquatic life make their introduction into environmental matrices a serious concern. Since these pollutants cannot be eliminated by current cleanup techniques, new treatment strategies must be developed. Because of its distinct structure, physicochemical characteristics, and wide range of possible uses, graphene has garnered significant interest as a novel kind of two-dimensional nanostructure. Graphene and its derivative forms have been widely studied for environmental cleanup and pollution reduction, primarily because of their exceptional chemical stability, extensive surface area, rapid electron mobility, superior thermal conductivity, and two-dimensional structure. Graphene functionalization techniques produce unique derivatives like graphene oxide (GO), reduced GO (rGO), and functional rGO (frGO) for diverse applications. This chapter reviews the use of graphene-derived hybrid micro/nanofibers for environmental remediation. It describes their physical, structural, and chemical properties, focusing on sustainable manufacturing, end-of-life recycling, and environmental safety assessments.
articles.summary_en: The chapter reviews graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, and functionalized graphene hybrid micro/nanofibers for removing industrial pollutants. It also considers sustainable manufacturing, recycling, and environmental-safety assessment, but reports no specific commercial deployment.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Based Functional Composites: Preparation, Self-Healing Systems and Applications
articles.title_en: Review Maps Graphene Functional Composites and Self-Healing Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene is a two-dimensional carbon nanomaterial with atomically thin layered structure. It shows notable mechanical stiffness, charge mobility, thermal conductivity and molecular barrier performance, making it a valuable reinforcing and functionalizing phase for advanced composite systems. Over the past decade, researchers have developed various graphene-incorporated functional composites for applications including self-healing polymers, electrochemical sensors, energy storage electrodes, separation membranes and structural laminates. This review examines mainstream synthesis routes and surface modification approaches for graphene and graphene oxide (GO), focusing on three self-healing composite platforms: polyurethane matrices, hydrogel networks and cementitious materials. For each system, fabrication methods, structure-property relationships and repair mechanisms are discussed. The review also covers applications of graphene-based materials in food safety sensing, lithium-ion battery anodes, water treatment membranes and aerospace structural composites. Despite progress, bottlenecks remain, including poor nanofiller dispersion, weak interfacial adhesion, batch-to-batch variability and high manufacturing cost. These issues limit translation from laboratory demonstrations to industrial use. Optimization strategies are proposed, including hierarchical structural design, precision interface engineering and scalable green manufacturing. This work provides a reference for performance optimization and practical application of graphene-based functional composites.
articles.summary_en: A review examines graphene and graphene oxide composites for self-healing polymers, hydrogels, cementitious materials, sensors, battery anodes, water-treatment membranes and aerospace structures. It identifies dispersion, interfacial adhesion, production consistency and cost as barriers to industrial translation, while highlighting scalable manufacturing and interface engineering as priorities.

articles.title_original: Advances and Potentials of Graphene Materials in Tendon-Bone Interface Healing: A Review
articles.title_en: Review Highlights Graphene’s Potential for Tendon–Bone Interface Healing
articles.excerpt_original: In the field of orthopedic sports medicine, the healing of the tendon-bone interface (TBI) has always been challenging. This is due to the unique gradient fibrocartilage transition zone structure of the TBI, which limits the gradient tissue regeneration ability from the tendon to the bone and easily leads to TBI regeneration disorders. This unsolved problem has always been widely concerned. Lowdimensional biological materials represented by graphene materials, due to their high specific surface area, good mechanical properties, excellent biocompatibility, bionic topological structure and multimodal regulation capabilities, provide new solutions for the regeneration of TBI. In this article, we focus on reviewing the biological characteristics of graphene materials, the potential research value of graphene materials in regulating cells related to TBI healing, the application prospects of graphene-based composite biomaterials in TBI, as well as the challenges and prospects faced, aiming to provide theoretical references for related research on TBI healing.
articles.summary_en: A review examines graphene materials and graphene-based composites for tendon–bone interface regeneration, focusing on their biocompatibility, mechanical properties, topology and ability to regulate relevant cells. The work identifies biomedical opportunities while noting unresolved challenges in translating these materials toward clinical healing applications.

articles.title_original: Interfacial Regulation of Wettability and Layered Bottom-Up Crystallization of Graphene-Supported Ni Nanodroplets
articles.title_en: Study Models Crystallization of Graphene-Supported Nickel Nanodroplets
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The solidification behavior of metallic nanodroplets on 2D material surfaces is critical for fabricating metal/carbon composites and regulating nanocrystalline microstructures. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the effect of Ni-C interfacial interaction strength on rapid solidification of graphene-supported Ni nanodroplets. We systematically analyzed wetting, thermal crystallization, local structure, crystallization distribution, and FCC/HCP layered enrichment. Stronger interactions reduce the contact angle and increase interfacial contact atoms, promoting droplet spreading and enlarging the Ni/graphene contact area. Average potential energy shifts upward in both onset and termination temperatures, implying enhanced coupling enables crystallization at elevated temperatures. Structural analysis shows weak interactions yield non-directional nucleation and growth, whereas strong interactions induce ordered structures near the interface that subsequently extend upward, exhibiting interface-associated bottom-up crystallization. The highest close-packed fraction resides in the middle of the nanoparticles, indicating that interface-induced crystallization, interfacial constraint, and free-surface effects jointly cause spatial nonuniformity. Overall, Ni-C interactions reshape the crystallization pathway, resulting in spatially nonuniform close-packed ordering and FCC/HCP layered enrichment in the final nanoparticle.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations show that stronger nickel–carbon interfacial interactions improve wetting and promote interface-associated, bottom-up crystallization. The findings could inform fabrication of graphene–nickel composites and control of nanocrystalline structure, but no company or commercial application is identified.

articles.title_original: Macroscopic Configurations of Graphene Electrodes for Flexible Supercapacitors: A Comparative Review
articles.title_en: Review Compares Graphene Electrode Architectures for Flexible Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: Currently, flexible wearable electronic devices are developing rapidly, so there is a need for lightweight, high-efficiency flexible energy storage devices. Graphene has a unique two-dimensional structure and excellent physicochemical properties, so it is a prominent candidate material for flexible supercapacitors. This paper presents a summary of the research advancements in one-dimensional fibers, two-dimensional films, and three-dimensional porous graphene macroscopic configurations, while comparing them based on structural attributes, mechanical flexibility, and electrochemical performance. According to this comparison, this paper discusses the selection strategy for suitable configurations in graphene-based flexible supercapacitor development, offering a guide for electrode design.
articles.summary_en: This review compares one-dimensional graphene fibers, two-dimensional films, and three-dimensional porous structures for flexible supercapacitor electrodes. It evaluates their structural, mechanical, and electrochemical characteristics to guide configuration selection for wearable energy-storage devices.

articles.title_original: Origami Folding Modulates Directional Thermal Transport in Pillared Graphene
articles.title_en: Origami Folding Tunes Thermal Transport in Pillared Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Pillared graphene can undergo origami-like folding under in-plane compression. Such folding reorients the graphene sheets and may change the heat transport pathway. Thus, the reverse nonequilibrium molecular dynamics method is used to investigate how in-plane compression affects directional thermal transport in pillared graphene at room temperature. Separate periodic supercells resolve heat transport along the in-plane and out-of-plane directions. Our results show that increasing the compressive strain to 0.26 reduces the in-plane thermal conductivity from 6.66 to 3.77 W m−1K−1 and increases the out-of-plane value from 1.30 to 2.02 W m−1K−1. Despite the out-of-plane conductivity increase, its area-weighted value remains close to the uncompressed reference, while the conductance proxies decrease by approximately 25% and 18% in the two directions. These results show that origami-like folding changes directional thermal transport in pillared graphene. The outcome of this study can provide insights into developing carbon nanomaterials with tunable thermal properties.
articles.summary_en: Molecular-dynamics simulations show that in-plane compression and origami-like folding reduce in-plane thermal conductivity while increasing out-of-plane conductivity. The findings suggest a route to tunable directional thermal transport in graphene-based nanomaterials.

articles.title_original: MXene‐Based Photodetectors: Progress and Prospects
articles.title_en: Review Maps MXene Advances in Photodetectors
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXenes, a novel class of 2D transition metal carbides, carbonitrides, and nitrides derived from layered MAX phases, have attracted considerable attention for future photodetector applications due to their unique structural, optical, and electronic properties. Their tunable surface terminations (–O, –OH, –F) and metallic conductivity enable precise modulation of work function and carrier dynamics, facilitating efficient charge transfer and reduced dark current when integrated into semiconductor junctions. This review systematically explores the impact of various synthesis methods, such as HF, in situ HF, electrochemical, and alkali‐assisted etching, on MXene morphology, surface chemistry, and interfacial quality, which are critical for device performance. Key material properties relevant to photodetection, including optical transparency, high carrier mobility, tunable plasmonic response, and adjustable work function, are thoroughly examined. Furthermore, the review underscores MXene role in diverse photodetector designs, highlighting its application as an electrode, charge transport, and active‐layer material. By correlating synthesis techniques with intrinsic properties and device performance, this review provides a comprehensive understanding of how MXene engineering can enhance responsivity, detectivity, and spectral range in optoelectronic systems. Finally, it addresses the current challenges and future opportunities for optimizing MXene‐based materials for high‐performance, broadband, and flexible photodetectors.
articles.summary_en: This review examines MXene synthesis, surface chemistry, and integration into photodetectors as electrodes, charge-transport layers, and active materials. It links material engineering to improvements in responsivity, detectivity, spectral range, and flexible broadband device performance, while identifying remaining optimization challenges.

articles.title_original: Controlling MXene termination ensembles for stability and performance
articles.title_en: Controlling MXene Surface Terminations for Stability and Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The promise of MXene surface chemistry lies in tuning T $$_{x}$$ x , yet the relevant design variable is not the identity of an individual surface terminating group but the ensemble of local surface environments. In M $$_{n+1}$$ n + 1 X $$_{n}$$ n T $$_{x}$$ x MXenes, where M is an early transition metal and X is C or N, T $$_{x}$$ x is treated here as a functional termination ensemble: the collection of local termination environments that exist across MXene surfaces. These environments are defined by chemical composition, binding-site geometry, coverage, spatial distribution, coordination, defects, intercalants, and edge structures. Because these ensembles evolve during synthesis, storage, processing, and operation, they determine whether MXenes remain structurally intact and functionally useful within application-specific performance–stability windows. We argue that predictive design requires computational approaches that move beyond idealized single-termination models by combining density functional theory, molecular dynamics, statistical sampling, surrogate models, and actively learned machine learning interatomic potentials to map termination ensembles under operating conditions. Coupled with synthesis–characterization feedback, this performance–stability framework links application-defined functions and operating windows to ensembles that can be installed, retained, or deliberately transformed while co-optimizing performance and stability.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose treating MXene surface chemistry as ensembles of local termination environments rather than isolated functional groups. They outline computational and experimental strategies to optimize these ensembles for application-specific performance and stability.

articles.title_original: MXene-Enabled Biomaterials for Wound Healing: Recent Advances, Mechanistic Insights, and Translational Prospects
articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene-Enabled Biomaterials for Wound Healing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The skin is the body’s largest organ and its primary barrier against chemical, radiological, and microbial challenges. When wound healing is impaired or delayed, patients face significant clinical risks, including severe and potentially life-threatening complications. To address these challenges, a wide range of advanced dressing technologies such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), hydrogels, fibers, nanoparticles, and enzyme-based systems has been developed to support tissue repair and prevent infection. Many of these dressings incorporate bioactive components, including antibiotics, nanoparticles, and growth factors, to enhance therapeutic efficacy. Among emerging strategies, bioactive inorganic nanoparticles have drawn increasing attention for their ability to reinforce the regenerative functions of wound dressings. MXene-based nanoparticles show strong potential owing to their electrical conductivity, hydrophilicity, antibacterial activity, and biocompatibility. These features make MXenes promising building blocks for next-generation wound care materials. This review summarizes recent advances in integrating MXenes into MOFs, hydrogels, fibers, nanoparticle systems, and enzyme-based platforms. It also discusses the key factors that shape their performance, outlines strategies to improve their therapeutic effectiveness, and identifies priority research directions for accelerating the development and clinical translation of MXene-enabled biomaterials for wound healing.
articles.summary_en: A review assesses MXene nanoparticles in wound-dressing platforms including hydrogels, fibers, metal-organic frameworks, and enzyme-based systems. It highlights conductivity, hydrophilicity, antibacterial activity, and biocompatibility while identifying priorities for therapeutic improvement and clinical translation.

articles.title_original: EFFECT OF ELECTROLYTE ON THE CHARGE STORAGE CHARACTERISTICS OF Mo2CTx MXene ELECTRODES FOR SUPERCAPACITORS
articles.title_en: Electrolyte Chemistry Controls Mo₂CTₓ MXene Supercapacitor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: In this work, Mo2CTx MXene was successfully synthesized via selective etching of the Ga layer from the Mo2Ga2C precursor using concentrated HF solution. Its electrochemical performance was systematically investigated in 1 M H2SO4, 1 M Na2SO4, and 1 M CH3COONa aqueous electrolytes. The results show that the charge storage behavior of Mo2CTx is strongly dependent on the electrolyte, with the highest specific capacitance achieved in 1 M H2SO4, reaching 70.47 F g-1 at 10 mV s-1 from CV and 103.50 F g-1 at 1 A g-1 from GCD, compared with 48.85 and 55.00 F g-1 in CH3COONa and 46.29 and 49.78 F g-1 in Na2SO4, respectively. The superior performance in H2SO4 is attributed to the high mobility of H⁺and more favorable ion transport kinetics, as supported by the lower Warburg coefficient. In addition, Mo2CTx exhibits good cycling stability, retaining 94.89%, 89.64%, and 73.57% of its initial capacitance after 5,000 cycles in H2SO4, Na2SO4, and CH3COONa, respectively. These findings demonstrate the critical role of electrolyte chemistry in governing charge storage, ion transport, and cycling stability of Mo2CTx MXene and provide insights for optimizing MXene-based supercapacitor electrodes.
articles.summary_en: 研究 shows that Mo₂CTₓ MXene electrodes achieve their highest capacitance and ion-transport performance in sulfuric acid electrolyte, outperforming sodium sulfate and sodium acetate. Cycling stability also varies substantially with electrolyte chemistry, highlighting electrolyte selection as a key factor in MXene supercapacitor design.

articles.title_original: Recognition-to-signal mechanisms in MXene quantum dots for metal-ion sensing
articles.title_en: MXene Quantum Dots Enable Mechanism-Based Metal-Ion Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: MXene quantum dots (MQDs) provide a chemically versatile platform for metal-ion sensing because their surface coordination environments, defect-associated states, and size-dependent electronic structure can couple molecular recognition to measurable optical responses. This review develops a mechanism-centered framework for understanding that coupling rather than treating sensing performance as a collection of isolated analytical metrics. It first examines how surface terminations, coordination-site accessibility, electronic-state organization, solvation, and interfacial binding thermodynamics define the recognition landscape of MQDs. It then analyzes how recognition events are translated into fluorescence or electrochemiluminescence responses through charge transfer, energy transfer, static or dynamic quenching, inner-filter effects, and related excited-state perturbations. Particular emphasis is placed on structure–property–signal relationships, mechanistic distinguishability, and trade-offs among sensitivity, selectivity, reversibility, and robustness. Evidence from reported metal-ion sensing systems is comparatively assessed to identify recurring design trends and limitations in mechanistic validation, cross-platform benchmarking, and real-matrix translation. The analysis indicates that future progress depends less on maximizing signal magnitude than on establishing reproducible coordination environments, experimentally resolved transduction pathways, and standardized performance criteria. This perspective positions MQD sensing as a recognition-to-signal engineering problem governed by coupled surface chemistry and excited-state dynamics.
articles.summary_en: This review examines how surface chemistry, defects, and size-dependent electronic structure in MXene quantum dots translate metal-ion recognition into fluorescence or electrochemiluminescence signals. It highlights the need for reproducible coordination environments, validated transduction mechanisms, and standardized testing for real-matrix applications.

articles.title_original: Selective nanoparticle capture from EUV photomasks via plasma and laser-assisted elastomer stamping
articles.title_en: Plasma- and Laser-Assisted Stamping Captures Nanoparticles from EUV Photomasks
articles.excerpt_original: Particles smaller than 50 nm on extreme ultraviolet (EUV) photomasks are printable defects, yet they lie below the practical limit of wet cleaning and of most dry cleaning routes, which also risk damaging the multilayer stack. We report a contact-based process in which a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp is brought into contact with a defective region and captures the target particle on separation, acting only on the area addressed. Oxygen-plasma treatment of the PDMS surface increases the transfer efficiency of metallic particles from approximately 20% to above 90%. In contrast, the same treatment reduces the transfer efficiency of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) particles from approximately 71% to 30%, demonstrating that plasma treatment provides material-dependent control rather than a universal enhancement of particle transfer. Continuous-wave 532 nm irradiation (≤50 mW) of a thin Pt absorbing layer embedded in the stamp produces localized thermal expansion, enabling conformal contact and improving particle transfer from trench-patterned substrates. Optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) confirm the absence of detectable elastomeric residue after separation, and the process is further demonstrated on an actual patterned EUV photo mask.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a localized PDMS stamping process for removing sub-50 nm particles from EUV photomasks, addressing defects that challenge conventional cleaning methods. Oxygen-plasma treatment raised metallic-particle transfer efficiency above 90%, while laser-induced thermal expansion improved conformal contact on patterned substrates; the process was demonstrated on an actual EUV photomask.

articles.title_original: Overcoming Contamination‐Induced Barriers: Ohmic Vertical Transport in Atomically Clean MoS 2 /Au Junctions
articles.title_en: Atomically Clean MoS₂–Gold Interfaces Enable Ohmic Vertical Transport
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The application of two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductors, such as monolayer MoS 2 , is limited by high contact resistance commonly attributed to interfacial barriers at metal contacts. Furthermore, the dependence of electrical conductivity on MoS 2 thickness remains unsettled, as both increasing and decreasing trends with layer number have been reported. Using conductive atomic force microscopy (CAFM), we measure local electrical transport in MoS 2 /Au junctions with contrasting interface cleanliness: pristine interfaces prepared under ultra‐high vacuum (UHV) and contaminated interfaces prepared by the widely used PDMS‐assisted transfer under ambient conditions. By comparing monolayer MoS 2 /Au junctions prepared under these contrasting conditions, we demonstrate that an atomically clean interface enables highly conductive, ohmic transport in the vertical CAFM geometry. Measurements on mono‐ and multilayer regions further show that interfacial contamination introduces a substantial transport barrier and can reverse the thickness dependence of electrical transport. We rationalize these findings using electrical transport simulations based on Kirchhoff's laws, identifying the interplay between MoS 2 /Au interfacial resistance and lateral current spreading within MoS 2 layers as the origin of the opposite thickness trends. Lastly, we show that local force‐mediated lamination on lightly contaminated contacts can recover pristine, ohmic contacts, offering a route toward nanoscale patterning.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that removing interfacial contamination enables highly conductive, ohmic vertical transport in MoS₂/gold junctions. The findings clarify how contamination and layer thickness affect contact resistance and suggest force-mediated lamination for nanoscale contact patterning.

articles.title_original: Thermal crystallization of amorphous InSe thin films: phase evolution and spatial inhomogeneity
articles.title_en: Study identifies optimal thermal crystallization window for InSe thin films
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Controlled crystallization of amorphous thin InSe films can be considered one of the key steps toward the development of scalable technologies for the production of 2D semiconductors for post-silicon electronics and optoelectronics. However, the optimization of thermal treatment conditions to obtain structurally homogeneous films remains challenging due to the formation of competing crystalline phases in the In–Se system. This work investigates the structural inhomogeneity that can develop during the thermal crystallization of InSe thin films, revealing a multistage phase evolution. X-ray diffraction analysis combined with Raman mapping was employed to investigate the crystallization behavior and spatial phase distribution at different annealing temperatures. As a result, optimal annealing conditions were identified for obtaining a predominantly single-phase β -InSe phase. The most homogeneous structure was obtained within the narrow annealing temperature range of 335 ± 5 °C for film with thickness of ∼250 nm. At lower temperature, the film consisted of β -InSe as the main phase with In 4 Se 3 inclusions as a secondary phase, whereas higher temperatures promoted the formation of γ -In 2 Se 3 inclusions within the main InSe phase. However, thicker films (∼540 nm) exhibited a different phase distribution under similar annealing conditions, particularly along the film depth. These findings highlight the complex phase evolution of amorphous InSe films and demonstrate that the optimal annealing conditions alone do not guarantee uniform crystallization throughout the films thickness.
articles.summary_en: Researchers mapped phase evolution and spatial inhomogeneity during thermal crystallization of amorphous InSe films. A narrow annealing range of 335 ± 5 °C produced predominantly single-phase β-InSe in ~250 nm films, while thickness-dependent variation limited uniform crystallization.

articles.title_original: Emulating isomerization with two-dimensional Coulomb crystals
articles.title_en: Two-Dimensional Coulomb Crystals Emulate Molecular Isomerization
articles.excerpt_original: Isomerization is a fundamental process in chemistry. We use a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal to emulate molecular isomerization and characterize its physical mechanisms. In our molecular analog, the externally controlled confining potential determines the crystal’s potential energy surface (PES), thereby playing the role that the molecular electronic state plays in determining the PES in a molecule. We focus on a crystal of six Ba + 138 ions exhibiting a region of bistability, and use a Monte Carlo simulation to extract the PES as a function of the trap aspect ratio. Experimentally, we prepare the ions in a stable isomer, quench the PES to populate a metastable isomer and use a configuration-resolved imaging to detect isomerization in real time. We measure isomers’ populations in the bistability region and compare them with a theoretical model to extract the crystal’s temperature. Moreover, we derive the transition rates from the measured transient times, thus providing a full characterization of the isomerization process. Our work sets a platform for emulating molecular processes, paving the way to study quantum superpositions of crystal configurations and control isomeric excitations in two-dimensional Coulomb crystals.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used a two-dimensional crystal of barium ions to emulate molecular isomerization, directly imaging transitions between stable and metastable configurations. The study measured populations, temperatures, and transition rates, establishing a platform for investigating molecular processes and controlled isomeric excitations.

articles.title_original: Observation of light-induced Haldane gap in graphene
articles.title_en: Researchers observe light-induced Haldane gap in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Symmetry and topology, encoded in electronic wavefunctions, play a central role in the electronic properties and emergent phenomena of quantum materials. While these properties are conventionally determined by the equilibrium Hamiltonian, strong optical fields offer a fundamentally different route by reshaping the Hamiltonian on ultrafast timescales, turning symmetry and topology into dynamically controllable degrees of freedom. Graphene provides a paradigmatic platform for realizing this concept, where circularly polarized light has long been predicted to dynamically break time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and open a topologically nontrivial gap at the Dirac point. Despite extensive experimental efforts, direct observation of this Dirac gap-the defining spectroscopic signature of the dynamical TRS-breaking induced topological phase-has remained missing. Here we directly observe this light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the gap emerges simultaneously with the optical field and exclusively under circularly polarized driving, directly linking its opening to dynamical TRS breaking. Together with Floquet theory, we identify the gap with a light-induced Haldane mass and reveal the associated nontrivial Floquet Berry curvature and Chern topology. By demonstrating dynamical TRS breaking in a prototypical non-magnetic material, our results establish optical driving as a route to ultrafast engineering of symmetry and topology, opening opportunities for dynamically tunable quantum matter beyond equilibrium.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly observe a light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy under circularly polarized light. The finding demonstrates dynamically controllable time-reversal symmetry breaking and Floquet topological behavior, with potential relevance to tunable quantum-materials research.

articles.title_original: l -Cysteine-Functionalized MXene Porous Scaffold-Based Phase Change Films for Efficient Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Cysteine-Functionalized MXene Phase-Change Films Improve Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Phase change materials (PCMs) hold great promise for thermal management, yet their low thermal conductivity and liquid leakage severely hinder practical applications. Herein, we designed a high-enthalpy phase change composite film (LMAP) based on l-Cysteine-functionalized MXene (l-MXene) and aramid nanofibers (ANFs). l-cysteine was bonded to MXene via covalent and coordination bonds, and further crosslinked with ANF through hydrogen bonds to form layered aerogel films with a porous scaffold structure, which was subsequently impregnated with polyethylene glycol (PEG). The unique porous layered architecture of LMAP-20 achieved a PEG loading of 86.71%, a phase-change enthalpy of 169.33 J/g, and a tensile strength of 17.26 MPa for favorable energy storage performance. Moreover, l-MXene nanosheets endowed LMAP-50 with a high thermal conductivity of 1.58 W/(m·K), which enabled outstanding thermal management and reduced the operating temperature of the LED chip by 21.4 °C. These results suggest that the l-MXene/ANF porous scaffold holds great potential for fabricating phase change composites with high thermal conductivity and suppressed leakage, which could be applied for efficient thermal management in advanced electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed porous MXene/aramid nanofiber films impregnated with polyethylene glycol, achieving high phase-change enthalpy, reduced leakage, and thermal conductivity up to 1.58 W/(m·K). The composite lowered an LED chip’s operating temperature by 21.4 °C, indicating potential for electronic-device thermal management.

articles.title_original: CVD Multilayer Boron Nitride-encapsulated graphene Solution-Gated Field-Effect Transistors for wearable and implantable biosensors
articles.title_en: CVD hBN Encapsulation Improves Graphene Biosensors for Neural Recording
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Great efforts are currently devoted to the development of graphene Solution-Gated Field-effect transistors (gSGFET) as sensors for biosensing applications and particularly, neural implants. Indeed, with the high carrier mobility of graphene, graphene-based sensors exhibit very high sensitivity and the easy integration of graphene in flexible devices is a clear advantage for implantable technologies by reducing rejection from biological tissues. However, despite the great performances already exhibited by gSGFETs for biosensing, this technology has not shown its full potential yet. This is due to the fact that since the graphene channel is in direct contact with the liquid medium, the carrier mobility, and consequently the sensitivity of a gSGFET, stays below its theoretical value and the sensors performances are subjected to stability issues. Hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) has been proved to be a key two-dimensional material that will enable to overcome carrier mobility limitations. Because the access to highly pure large scale-hBN is challenging, we tested here whether more accessible lower-quality commercial Chemical Vapor Deposited Multilayer BN could still be successfully used to improve gSGFETs sensitivity for neural recordings. We demonstrate that even when using a commercial multilayer BN, the performances of gSGFET sensors can be improved to enable neural recording.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated that commercial multilayer chemical-vapor-deposited boron nitride can improve the sensitivity and performance stability of graphene solution-gated field-effect transistors. The approach supports wearable and implantable biosensing, including neural recordings, despite using lower-quality hBN material.

articles.title_original: Interface-Engineered Bismuthene/PCN-222 Heterojunctions for the Visible-Light Photoredox C–H Arylation of (Hetero)arenes
articles.title_en: Bismuthene–MOF Heterojunction Enhances Visible-Light C–H Arylation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The photocatalytic performance of semiconductor metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is often limited by rapid charge-carrier recombination, insufficient visible-light absorption, and weak interfacial interactions in heterojunctions, highlighting the need for synthetic strategies that enable strong interfacial coupling for efficient charge transfer. Herein, we rationally engineered MOF/2D semiconductor heterojunctions through two different assembly strategies: physical mixing (P) and in situ interfacial growth (I). The heterojunctions were formulated by using bismuthene (Biene) and PCN-222 MOF via either mechanical blending (Biene/PCN-222(P)) or chemical integration (Biene/PCN-222(I)). In the visible-light-driven C–H arylation of (hetero)arenes, Biene/PCN-222(I) exhibited markedly superior photocatalytic activity compared with the individual components and the physically assembled counterpart while also demonstrating a broad substrate scope. Notably, excellent catalytic performance was maintained even for benzene, which is one of the most challenging substrates. The superior performance of the in situ-assembled Biene/PCN-222(I) heterojunction is attributed to the formation of a strongly coupled interface and complex type-II band alignment, which synergistically suppress charge-carrier recombination and promote directional interfacial charge migration, thereby improving charge-separation and charge-transfer efficiencies under visible-light irradiation. Mechanistic studies further confirmed the generation of aryl-radical intermediates during the photocatalytic process, validating the single electron transfer pathway.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered bismuthene/PCN-222 heterojunctions using physical mixing and in situ interfacial growth. The in situ structure delivered superior photocatalytic activity, including for benzene, by strengthening interfacial charge transfer and suppressing recombination.

articles.title_original: Ferroelectric-substrate coupling modulates hydrovoltaic droplet-induced electrical signals on graphene
articles.title_en: Ferroelectric substrates tune droplet-induced signals in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Hydrovoltaic electricity generation at graphene-liquid interfaces is sensitive to both the electronic state of graphene and the electrostatic environment at the interface. However, how remanent ferroelectric polarization pre-conditions the electronic state of graphene before droplet contact, and how this state is related to the subsequent electrical response, remains unclear. Here, we use electrically pre-poled LiTaO 3 (LTO) and LiNbO 3 (LNO) ferroelectric substrates to electrostatically pre-condition graphene before liquid contact. Kelvin probe force microscopy reveals clear polarization-dependent shifts in graphene work function. Positive polarization produces a relatively electron-rich state, whereas negative polarization shifts graphene toward a more hole-rich state. Despite these distinct electronic states, the hydrovoltaic response does not follow a universal polarization-dependent voltage ordering across LiTaO 3 and LiNbO 3 , indicating that graphene carrier modulation alone cannot account for the generated response. Transient measurements further reveal strongly polarization- and substrate-dependent changes in the rise and decay time constant, indicating that ferroelectric polarization influences not only the signal magnitude but also transient interfacial charge dynamics. Repeated droplet exposure and subsequent cleaning produce partially reversible changes in the electrical response, while long-term ambient aging substantially reduces the polarization-dependent work-function contrast. Together, these results establish an experimental link between remanent ferroelectric polarization, the pre-contact electronic state of graphene, and the subsequent droplet-induced electrical response. Ferroelectric substrates therefore provide a substrate-side strategy for regul
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that remanent polarization in lithium tantalate and lithium niobate substrates changes graphene’s work function and modulates hydrovoltaic droplet-response dynamics. The findings identify ferroelectric substrate engineering as a route to control graphene–liquid interfacial electrical signals, although responses vary by substrate.

articles.title_original: Research Progress on Graphene-Based Sensing Mechanism and Devices in Food Safety and Food Freshness
articles.title_en: Review Surveys Graphene-Based Sensors for Food Safety and Freshness
articles.excerpt_original: Food safety is a major basic guarantee for both public health and life safety in modern industrial society. The freshness and safety testing of food are like an indispensable protective wall. Traditional analysis methods such as chromatography, mass spectrometry are cumbersome to operate. There are also limitations such as high cost and time-consuming. This paper clarifies the adsorption mechanism of graphene-based on the relevant gases generated by food spoilage and the liquid sensing mechanism of additives that endanger food safety, summarizing different modification methods. It sorts out the sensor devices and specific applications adapted to food safety and food freshness, looking forward to the challenges and future development trends in this field.
articles.summary_en: The review examines graphene’s gas-adsorption mechanisms for detecting food spoilage and liquid-sensing mechanisms for hazardous additives. It also summarizes material modifications, device architectures, applications, and remaining development challenges.

articles.title_original: Detection and Inhalation Hazard Assessment of Wear Particles Arising From Abrasion of Market‐relevant Graphene Reinforced Composites
articles.title_en: Study Finds Limited Acute Respiratory Toxicity from Abraded Graphene–Epoxy Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Commercial products incorporating graphene-based two-dimensional (2D) nanosheets are increasingly developed to enhance mechanical, thermal, and electrical performance. Potential release of inhalable particles during manufacturing or end-of-life processing, however, raises concerns regarding respiratory health. This study explored the pulmonary cytotoxicity and immunomodulatory activity of airborne particles generated by mechanical abrasion of industrially relevant few-layer graphene (FLG) reinforced epoxy composites. A multimodal analytical strategy combining high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, Raman microscopy, and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry enabled reliable detection and spatial mapping of FLG in pristine and abraded composites. Abrasion predominantly produced composite fragments in which FLG remained embedded, with no indication of protruding or freely released FLG nanosheets. Across advanced bronchial and alveolar epithelial air-liquid interface models, neither abraded epoxy nor FLG-epoxy particles induced cytotoxic or pro-inflammatory responses. A moderate reduction of mucociliary clearance was observed only at high exposure doses of abraded epoxy particles, without amplification by FLG reinforcement. As-produced FLG triggered strong TNF-α secretion in alveolar macrophages, whereas abraded FLG-epoxy particles elicited minimal responses. Overall, the findings indicate limited acute respiratory toxicity associated with inhalation of fragments released from FLG-based epoxy composites under production and end-of-life scenarios.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that abrasion mainly produced epoxy fragments with graphene remaining embedded, rather than freely released nanosheets. The particles caused minimal cytotoxic or inflammatory responses in airway models, though high doses of epoxy fragments moderately reduced mucociliary clearance.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Multifunctional Optimization of Carbon Fiber/Phenolic Composites via a Hierarchical ZnO @C/Graphene Interface Design
articles.title_en: ZnO–Graphene Interface Boosts Composite Strength, EMI Shielding and Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Carbon fiber reinforced phenolic resin matrix composites (CP) are widely used in the field of electronic devices, which require superior mechanical characteristics, electromagnetic shielding capability, as well as thermal management performance. Optimizing the interfacial architecture offers a viable strategy to simultaneously enhance these key properties. In this work, carbon‐coated ZnO‐graphene (ZnO@C‐GE) was successfully introduced into CP. ZnO@C‐GE constructs a hierarchically porous architecture that synergistically enhances mechanical interlocking (via resin infiltration), electromagnetic wave attenuation (through multi‐scale scattering), and thermal transport (by reducing interfacial voids). Consequently, the tensile strength of ZnO@C‐GE reinforced CP (ZnO@C‐GE‐CP) reaches 168.8 ± 1.7 MPa, representing a 51% enhancement over pure CP. This structural design simultaneously achieves an X‐band electromagnetic interference shielding efficiency (EMI SE) of 43 dB (47% improvement) and thermal conductivity of (8.47 ± 0.11) × 10 −1 W(m·K) −1 (71% increase), attributed to optimized electromagnetic dissipation pathways and reduced interfacial thermal resistance between carbon fibers and resin. These multifunctional advances position ZnO@C‐GE‐CP as a promising candidate for next‐generation electromagnetic shielding.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced carbon-coated ZnO–graphene into carbon-fiber/phenolic composites, achieving 168.8 MPa tensile strength, 43 dB X-band EMI shielding, and 0.847 W/m·K thermal conductivity. The hierarchical porous interface improves mechanical interlocking, electromagnetic attenuation, and thermal transport, indicating potential for multifunctional electronic and shielding components.

articles.title_original: Coherent MXene/metal interface builder
articles.title_en: Tool Builds and Relaxes MXene–Metal Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Builds an MXene/metal interface in one orthogonal box, relaxes it with a MACE machine-learned potential and compares the built and relaxed structures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced a computational interface builder that constructs MXene–metal structures in a standardized cell. It uses a MACE machine-learned potential to relax the structures and compare the initial and optimized configurations.

articles.title_original: Hybrid Electrode Based on Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride for Fast Electrophysiological Signal Exploration
articles.title_en: Exploratory hBN Spin-Defect Electrode Proposed for Fast Electrophysiology
articles.excerpt_original: NV-NEUROBUS / hBN-VB Hybrid Electrode Based on Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride for Fast Electrophysiological Signal Exploration Author: Jean-Yves Lozac’h de KerpertAffiliation: Independent Researcher, FranceDate: 30 October 2026Version: 0.3Status: Exploratory conceptual preprint, not peer-reviewed. Abstract This work proposes an exploratory hybrid electrode architecture combining a conventional conductive interface with a functional hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layer containing negatively charged boron vacancy spin defects ((V_B^-)). The objective is to investigate whether optically addressable spin defects could provide an additional measurement modality alongside conventional electrophysiological recording. Two transduction mechanisms are considered: Direct electrical coupling through a potential Stark effect on the spectroscopic properties of (V_B^-) defects. Electromechanical transduction involving a piezoelectric layer and a magnetostrictive material, using the inverse magnetostrictive effect (Villari effect), followed by optical detection of magnetic changes through ODMR. The exploratory application concerns fast electrophysiological events, particularly hippocampal ripple-like activity in the 80–150 Hz frequency range. The manuscript describes the proposed architecture, preliminary physical modelling, engineering constraints, metrological considerations and a comparative experimental protocol. A preliminary sensitivity analysis indicates that direct detection of weak biological signals remains challenging. A first non-biological proof of concept using controlled electrical signals and high-quality exfoliated hBN is therefore proposed. No biological detection capability, experimental validation or superiority over conventional electrodes is claimed. The p
articles.summary_en: A conceptual preprint proposes a hybrid electrode using boron-vacancy spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride to complement conventional electrophysiological recording. The architecture could enable optical sensing of fast signals, but the work remains unvalidated and reports no biological detection or performance advantage.

articles.title_original: Feasibility study of femtosecond-laser-induced folding in hexagonal boron nitride using simulation and microscopy evidence
articles.title_en: Study Demonstrates Feasibility of Laser-Folded Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Femtosecond-laser-induced folding offers a promising route to realise functional three-dimensional structures from two-dimensional materials, and the processing has the advantages of a small heat-affected zone, high precision, and high efficiency. Confirm whether the ultrafast laser excitation generates sufficient thermal stress to fold hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) through experiments. This paper explores the feasibility of this folding mode by building a multi-physics simulation system in COMSOL and providing corresponding microscopy data. For computational efficiency and to ensure the physical accuracy of the results, a 2D axisymmetric transient thermal-structural coupled model was built, and then a cross-section was rotated to generate a 3D cylindrical model. Additionally, a single 50 nm layer of h-BN was used instead of a multi-layer structure to simplify the calculation of thermal stress evolution. According to the results of the simulation, rapid addition of energy leads to melting and stress redistribution, and thus an upward deformation of the edge occurs. The two basic requirements for feasibility are shown in the figure and height judgment. The model-modified alterations to the shape were consistent with the experimental optical and atomic-force microscopy data. The simulation shows that the folded structure has a height of about 117 nm; this is close to the measured value of about 100 nm in the experiment. Combining the above results, it can be seen that ultrafast laser pulses can generate the necessary thermal-mechanical conditions for folding h-BN; thus, laser-driven h-BN origami is feasible for micro- and nanofabrication.
articles.summary_en: Simulations and microscopy indicate that femtosecond-laser pulses can generate sufficient thermal stress to fold 50 nm hexagonal boron nitride into three-dimensional structures. The predicted fold height of approximately 117 nm closely matched the experimentally measured height of about 100 nm, supporting applications in micro- and nanofabrication.

articles.title_original: Theoretical anatomy of altermagnetic α-MnTe from magnetism to triple-resistance states
articles.title_en: Theoretical study predicts triple-resistance states in altermagnetic α-MnTe
articles.excerpt_original: α-MnTe is among the earliest discovered altermagnets with experimental evidence of A-type antiferromagnetic order above room temperature and spin-split bands. Here, we conduct a theoretical investigation of its magnetism based on the general symmetry-adaptive tensorial spin model, which not only confirms a Néel temperature of 340 K induced by the dominant 1st and 3rd nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchanges, but also the hexagonal planar Néel vector polarization of the ground state due to both the single-ion and the two-ion anisotropies. The 6-fold rotation symmetry along z prohibits an in-plane easy axis when only considering rank-2 and rank-4 interactions, revealing the continuous ground state degeneracy. Subsequently, we show that the triple-resistance states can be realized by adopting MnTe as the barrier in the sandwiched magnetic tunnel junctions. By deliberately matching the Brillouin zone-resolved spin transport of both the barrier and the electrode, tunneling magnetoresistance up to ~5300% is obtained. Our work not only provides a fine database of the magnetism and transmission for MnTe, but also sheds light on the application in high-density spintronic memory devices.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical modeling identifies the magnetic ground state of α-MnTe and predicts tunneling magnetoresistance of up to approximately 5300% when MnTe is used as a barrier in magnetic tunnel junctions. The findings indicate potential applications in high-density spintronic memory devices.

articles.title_original: Multiamino Polydiacetylene-Mediated Interfacial Engineering of Boron Nitride Nanosheet/Polyimide Composites for Low-Dielectric Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Boron Nitride–Polyimide Composite Delivers Low-Dielectric Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The rapid advancement of high-frequency and highly integrated semiconductor devices urgently calls for dielectric materials that combine high thermal conductivity, low dielectric constant, and excellent thermal stability. Herein, multiamino polydiacetylene-functionalized boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS@MAPDA) have been incorporated into a MAPDA-containing polyimide matrix to improve filler–matrix interfacial coupling. The functionalized nanosheets exhibit high aspect ratios, few lattice defects, high yields, and excellent dispersion in the PI-MAPDA matrix. At a filler loading of only 7.5 wt %, the PI‑MAPDA/BNNS@MAPDA‑7.5 composite film achieves an in‑plane thermal conductivity of 1.67 W m–1 K–1, representing a 422% enhancement over pristine PI‑MAPDA. Benefiting from the ultralow polarizability of fluorinated groups and the strengthened interfacial coupling, the nanocomposite simultaneously maintains a low dielectric constant of 2.20 and a low dielectric loss tangent (tanδ) of 0.0066 at 1 MHz, alongside a volume resistivity of 9.7 × 1011 Ω cm. The density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that MAPDA functionalization enhances interfacial affinity and energy transfer, while molecular dynamics (MD) simulations elucidate its influence on thermal conductivity and dielectric properties. The Hashin–Shtrikman (HS) model analysis further confirms the positive role of interface regulation in thermal conductivity enhancement. MAPDA-mediated interphase engineering, through multisite anchoring to BNNS and strong chemical affinity with the PI matrix, provides an effective route to promote interfacial heat transfer while suppressing interfacial polarization at low filler loading. This material provides a promising solution for advanced electronic insulation and packa
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers engineered functionalized boron nitride nanosheets into a polyimide matrix, achieving 1.67 W m−1 K−1 in-plane thermal conductivity at 7.5 wt% filler loading. The composite retained a low dielectric constant of 2.20 and low dielectric loss, indicating potential for insulated high-frequency semiconductor packaging.

articles.title_original: Topologically Protected Edge States in a Single Flux Qubit
articles.title_en: Single Flux Qubit Demonstrates Topologically Protected Edge States
articles.excerpt_original: We show that topological edge states can be realized in a simple superconducting circuit composed of an inductively shunted flux qubit. The Josephson potential of that qubit forms a honeycomb lattice similar to the case of graphene. The additional shunting element produces a quartic potential along one flux direction, which effectively creates a boundary in flux space. We map analytically the low-energy dynamics of the circuit to an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chain, in which a quartic potential is added to the usual SSH Hamiltonian. This mapping is confirmed by numerical simulations of the full superconducting circuit. We argue that chiral symmetry still holds for the edge states of the extended model around a chiral point in parameter space. Close to this point, we numerically find that edge states in our superconducting circuit are topologically protected against perturbations that obey chiral symmetry, as is the case for charge noise. Our results show that topological effects previously thought to occur in multi-qubit systems, such as protection against decoherence, can also be found in much simpler single superconducting qubits.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically and numerically show that an inductively shunted flux qubit can support topologically protected edge states. The work maps the circuit to an extended SSH chain and suggests decoherence protection against chiral-symmetry-preserving perturbations, including charge noise, without requiring multiple qubits.

articles.title_original: Andreev-Enhanced Conductance in a Bilayer Graphene Quantum Point Contact
articles.title_en: Bilayer Graphene Quantum Point Contact Shows Andreev-Enhanced Conductance
articles.excerpt_original: Quantum point contacts provide a platform for probing mode-dependent Andreev reflection. Here, we demonstrate Andreev-enhanced conductance in a gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum point contact coupled to a superconducting aluminum electrode. Electrostatic gating enables sequential mode occupation, verified by normal-state conductance quantization. In the superconducting state, the conductance is enhanced within the conductance plateaus, while the enhancement decreases between plateaus, consistent with the nonlinear transmission dependence of Andreev reflection. The enhancement yields effective transmission probabilities up to 0.9, and extends over a bias window of approximately 140 $μ$V, which we associate with a proximity-induced superconducting gap, close to the gap of the aluminum film. For in-plane fields, the enhancement persists up to the critical field, and the bias window follows the spectral gap predicted by Abrikosov-Gor'kov theory. In contrast, perpendicular fields suppress the enhancement approximately linearly from zero field, deviating from homogeneous pair breaking and indicative of flux penetration.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate gate-controlled Andreev-enhanced conductance in a bilayer graphene quantum point contact coupled to a superconducting aluminum electrode. The device reaches effective transmission probabilities of up to 0.9 and reveals field-dependent proximity superconductivity, supporting graphene-based quantum and superconducting electronics research.

articles.title_original: Selecting Ion Beam Energy for Defect Engineering in h -BN and Graphene
articles.title_en: Study Guides Ion-Beam Defect Engineering in Graphene and h-BN
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Computational guidance for selective defect engineering in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and graphene by ion implantation is essential for the development of single-atom catalysts, single-photon emitters, and quantum sensors based on these two-dimensional materials. We use spin-polarized ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to predict the minimum energy of ion irradiation leading to atom ejection from h-BN and graphene. The study spans 64 elements of the Periodic Table from He to Hg, excluding lanthanides, and it investigates the irradiation conditions for direct single-step implantation. We show that in the low ion energy regime (tens of electronvolts), the implantation outcome is determined by chemical interactions between an incident ion and the target atom in a monolayer. Our results are aimed at guiding experiments on the controlled generation of vacancies and dopant centers in h-BN and graphene by choosing an appropriate ion for irradiation and tuning its kinetic energy.
articles.summary_en: Computational simulations identify minimum ion energies for atom ejection and implantation in graphene and hexagonal boron nitride across 64 elements. The findings could help researchers tune vacancies and dopant centers for quantum sensors, single-photon emitters, and single-atom catalysts.

articles.title_original: From plasma to photons: engineering PECVD-grown graphene for next-generation light-based medical devices
articles.title_en: PECVD graphene enables lower-temperature photonic and biomedical device design

Engineers in both the photonic and biomedical fields have known about this unique combination for nearly twenty years; however, most of those possibilities are not supported by any sort of design tool because there has been no systematic study which provided optical transmission/absorption data along with thermal conductivity data from the exact same piece of material grown under identical conditions. We fill that gap here. The location of the UV dip is also consistent with theoretical predictions. Thermal conductivity decreases from approximately 3000 W/m-K at 300 K to around 800 W/m-K at 1000 K and follows an Umklapp scattering law but does so continuously throughout the temperature range investigated.
