articles.summary_en: Researchers characterized optical transmission, absorption, and thermal conductivity from the same PECVD-grown graphene samples. Large-area monolayers produced on copper foils at 600–800°C showed 97.7% visible transmission and thermal conductivity declining from about 3,000 W/m-K at 300 K to 800 W/m-K at 1,000 K, providing design data for light-based medical devices.

articles.title_original: Scalable Melt-Spun Polyethylene/Boron Nitride Fabric Integrating Radiative and Nonradiative Cooling Effects for Personal Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Melt-Spun Polyethylene–Boron Nitride Fabric Enables Radiative and Conductive Cooling
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract With the escalating global energy crisis and environmental challenges, radiative cooling textiles have emerged as a promising energy-free thermal management solution. However, existing cooling fabrics primarily focus on enhancing optical properties like solar reflectance and infrared emissivity, often neglecting the critical role of nonradiative heat dissipation (conduction and convection) while also facing challenges in scalability, durability, and comfort. To address these limitations, this study presents a scalably manufactured polyethylene/boron nitride (HDPE/BN) composite fabric fabricated via industrial melt spinning and weaving. By uniformly incorporating BN sheets into HDPE fibers, the composite fabric achieves enhanced solar reflectivity (86%) and mid-infrared emissivity (89.3%) due to the high refractive index, efficient Mie scattering, and intrinsic infrared absorption features of BN. More importantly, it exhibits enhanced in-plane thermal conductivity (7.73 ± 0.18 W·m–1·K–1) while maintaining breathability, complementing the nonradiative cooling effects. Experimental results demonstrate that the fabric provides temperature reductions of 3.7 °C (daytime) and 2.7 °C (nighttime) in simulated building cooling tests, and 3.9 °C (daytime) and 1.6 °C (nighttime) in simulated human skin tests. This work highlights the importance of integrating optical and thermal management properties, providing a scalable manufacturing route of high-performance personal cooling textiles for practical applications.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers developed a scalable melt-spun and woven HDPE/boron nitride fabric combining high solar reflectance, infrared emissivity, and in-plane thermal conductivity. The material reduced temperatures in simulated building and human-skin tests, indicating potential for personal thermal-management textiles.

articles.title_original: Complex Refractive Index Determination Via Microspectroscopy Through Magnifying Optics: Challenges and Opportunities
articles.title_en: Microspectroscopy Enables Refractive-Index Measurement of Micrometer-Scale Materials
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT For the design and optimization of optoelectronic devices, accurate knowledge of the complex refractive indices of the constituent materials is essential. Herein, we present a fast and nondestructive approach for the extraction of the refractive indices from reflectance and transmittance spectra of samples with lateral dimensions down to the micrometer scale. Microspectroscopy, combining an optical microscope and a spectrometer, enables the assessment of the optical response of multilayer stacks using high‐magnification optics with correspondingly large numerical apertures. Employing a numerical formalism explicitly accounting for the influence of the numerical aperture allows for wavelength‐by‐wavelength retrieval of the refractive index with subsequent refinement by dispersion modeling. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method for large‐area, homogeneous, optically incoherent samples such as transparent glasses and absorbing 4H‐SiC, for a thin film on a glass substrate, and for mechanically exfoliated flakes of highly oriented pyrolytic graphite and , as representatives of uniaxial and biaxial optical anisotropy. The proposed approach provides a cost‐effective proof of concept for retrieving optical constants of microscale samples under arbitrary numerical apertures. The case of graphite highlights the limitation for discerning the out‐of‐plane optical constants due to reduced sensitivity. Finally, we discuss paths to probe out‐of‐plane anisotropy.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a nondestructive method for extracting complex refractive indices from microscale samples using reflectance and transmittance spectra while accounting for microscope numerical aperture. Demonstrations include transparent glass, absorbing 4H-SiC, thin films, and anisotropic graphite flakes, with limitations identified for measuring out-of-plane optical constants.

articles.title_original: Fire-Fighting Systems in Semiconductor Chiller Buildings Using A Bim Framework: A Review
articles.title_en: BIM Review Highlights Fire-Safety Coordination Needs in Semiconductor Chiller Buildings
articles.excerpt_original: Semiconductor manufacturing facilities depend on highly reliable utility infrastructure, including chiller buildings that support continuous process cooling. A fire in such a facility can threaten personnel, critical equipment, production continuity and the wider supply chain. Fire-protection design therefore requires careful coordination among sprinkler networks, standpipes, pumps, valves, pipe supports, building structure and other mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) services. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) computer-aided design drawings remain useful for drafting but provide limited spatial insight and can make interdisciplinary coordination and revision control difficult. This review examines the application of Building Information Modeling (BIM) to the design and coordination of fire-fighting systems, with particular emphasis on conversion of 2D AutoCAD layouts into a fabrication-oriented three-dimensional (3D) model for a semiconductor chiller building. Literature on BIM-based fire safety, sprinkler design, MEP modelling, automation, clash detection and model-based documentation is synthesized to identify practical benefits and persistent limitations. A workflow using Autodesk Revit, Navisworks and Dynamo is discussed, including model setup, component placement, coordination, standards-based review and production of schedules and drawings. The review indicates that BIM can improve visualization, information consistency and early identification of spatial conflicts; however, geometric coordination alone does not establish hydraulic adequacy or full code compliance. articles.summary_en: A review finds that BIM can improve visualization, information consistency and early clash detection when designing fire-fighting systems for semiconductor chiller buildings. It cautions that BIM-based geometric coordination does not ensure hydraulic adequacy or code compliance, which still requires validated inputs and qualified professional review.

articles.title_original: Potentials of individual atoms by convergent beam electron diffraction
articles.title_en: CBED method extracts individual-atom scattering potentials in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: In convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) on two-dimensional (2D) materials, the intensity distributions within the individual CBED spots map the local atomic arrangements within the probed region. In this study we demonstrate that the average intensities within the CBED spots essentially depend on the scattering parameters by a single atom, thus, offering the possibility of the direct measurement of such parameters. Scattering potential of an individual atom can be approximated by the Gaussian function and its parameters, the standard deviation and the maximal phase shift, can be recovered from the ratio of the intensities in the zero- and higher orders spots in CBED pattern. In order to demonstrate this, we simulated CBED patterns and extracted the atomic scattering parameters from such patterns. In the simulated examples, no weak phase object approximation is applied and the proposed method provides accurate results even for materials with large phase shifts up to 1.5 rad, as for example tungsten. The scattering parameters recovered from the experimental CBED patterns of graphene and twisted graphene-hBN structure show good agreement with the theoretically obtained values.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that convergent beam electron diffraction can recover individual-atom scattering parameters from intensity ratios in diffraction patterns. Simulations and measurements on graphene and twisted graphene–hBN agree with theoretical values, including for materials with large phase shifts.

articles.title_original: H-BCN Quantum Dots as Potential 10B Carriers and Imaging Tools for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) Applications
articles.title_en: BCN Quantum Dots Show Potential for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Boron Carbon Nitride (BCN) is a ternary compound exhibiting properties that lie between those of conductive graphene and insulating boron nitride. Numerous theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that hexagonal BCN (h-BCN) exhibits unique optical, electrical, mechanical, and thermal properties, along with high chemical inertness and biocompatibility, making it a promising material for a wide range of applications. Given their high volumetric boron content, we evaluated the potential of h-BCN nanomaterials as vectors for delivering and accumulating 10B within cells, thereby enabling effective cancer treatment via targeted neutron irradiation for BNCT. In this work, we investigated the synthesis and characterization of h-BCN quantum dots (BCN-QDs) and assessed their potential as 10B carriers and imaging tools. Fluorescence microscopy and intracellular neutron autoradiography confirmed the internalization of BCN-QDs in vitro and their distribution within the cell population. BCN-QDs were selectively internalized in HeLa cells, resulting in high 10B concentrations and demonstrating their potential as 10B carriers for BNCT applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers evaluated hexagonal boron carbon nitride quantum dots as boron-10 carriers and imaging tools for BNCT. In vitro studies found selective uptake by HeLa cells and high intracellular boron concentrations, but the findings remain preclinical.

articles.title_original: Photonic Crystal Integrated Graphene-Silicon Schottky Diodes for Resonant Infrared Photodetection
articles.title_en: Photonic-Crystal Graphene–Silicon Diodes Enable Narrowband Infrared Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Narrowband infrared (IR) photodetection has become a critical technology for the next generation of smart low-power photodetectors. In this work, we present a device based on a graphene-silicon Schottky junction with narrowband response in the short-wave IR (SWIR) regime. Integrating a photonic crystal (PhC) slab in the device enables a wavelength dependant tailoring of graphene absorption. The devices were characterized by photocurrent measurement, which was enhanced more than two orders of magnitude by the PhC integration. The sharp enhancements obtained can also be predicted by numerical simulation. This approach offers a highly scalable, tunable, CMOS-compatible architecture for narrowband IR photodetection, paving the way for next-generation, low-power IR sensors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated a photonic-crystal slab into graphene–silicon Schottky photodiodes to tailor graphene absorption for short-wave infrared detection. The approach increased photocurrent by more than two orders of magnitude and offers a tunable, CMOS-compatible architecture for low-power IR sensors.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Derived Nanomaterials for Wastewater Treatment: Bridging Laboratory Performance and Practical Feasibility
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Graphene Nanomaterials for Scalable Wastewater Treatment
articles.excerpt_original: Rapid industrialization and urbanization have increased the discharge of complex pollutants into aquatic systems, posing significant environmental and public health challenges. Conventional wastewater treatment technologies often fail to remove trace contaminants such as pharmaceuticals, heavy metals, and emerging organic compounds. Graphene-based materials, including graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, and graphene quantum dots, have emerged as promising candidates due to their high surface area, tunable surface chemistry, mechanical robustness, and unique electronic properties, enabling diverse removal mechanisms such as adsorption, catalysis, and membrane filtration. Laboratory studies have shown that these materials can achieve superior pollutant removal efficiencies; however, their large-scale implementation remains limited, highlighting the gap between laboratory performance and industrial feasibility.This review provides a structured assessment of graphene-based materials for wastewater treatment. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature review covering 2010–2024 was conducted, with emphasis on the latest 2025 studies addressing techno-economic and industrial feasibility. The review examines the types of graphene materials, their physicochemical properties, and functionalization strategies, followed by critical evaluation of their applications in removing various contaminants. Key research gaps, including aggregation, fouling, regeneration loss, toxicity, and lack of standardized protocols, are discussed. The techno-economic and industrial feasibility section analyzes production costs, scalability, energy requirements, and lifecycle considerations. Finally, future perspectives on AI-guided material design, smart membranes, and regulatory framework
articles.summary_en: A systematic review finds graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, and graphene quantum dots effective for removing pharmaceuticals, heavy metals, and other contaminants through adsorption, catalysis, and membrane filtration. It identifies aggregation, fouling, regeneration losses, toxicity, cost, scalability, and inconsistent standards as barriers to industrial deployment.

articles.title_original: Perspectives on Graphene-Based Materials in Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Fuel Cells: Improved Membrane Electrode Assembly and Sustainable Biographene Alternatives
articles.title_en: Review assesses graphene-based materials for improved fuel-cell assemblies
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are energy conversion devices that harness clean energy from electrochemical reactions, consistent with Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7). The core of PEMFCs, known as the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), is where the major processes occur and is highly dependent on the material used. Therefore, the selection of materials for MEA development is vital as inefficient materials may lead to reduced performance. In this context, one material that stands out is graphene, a carbon allotrope, owing to its good mechanical and electrochemical properties. Hence, this review aims to highlight recent findings on the development of graphene-based MEAs for improved PEMFC performance. Systematically arranged according to the three major components in the MEA, this review focuses on graphene-based diffusion layers, catalysts, and membranes, in which the first, despite gaining attention in fuel cell research, is usually excluded from the other two in review discussions. Additionally, this paper addresses the current barriers and future potential of graphene-based MEA studies, particularly the potential of biomass-derived graphene or biographene development. Overall, the discussions on graphene-based MEAs presented in this paper can be a beneficial guide for future research related to graphene development to enhance MEA performance in PEMFCs.
articles.summary_en: A review examines graphene-based diffusion layers, catalysts, and membranes for polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells. It highlights biomass-derived biographene as a potential sustainable option while identifying performance and development barriers; no specific companies are named.

articles.title_original: MXene‐Integrated Composites for Next‐Generation Photoelectrochemical Molecular Diagnostics
articles.title_en: MXene Composites Advance Photoelectrochemical Molecular Diagnostics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXenes, a family of two‐dimensional (2D) materials known for their characteristic electrical, optical, and surface properties, have emerged as promising candidates for advancing the performance of photoelectrochemical (PEC) biosensing technologies. When integrated into composites, including carbon‐based materials, metal nanoparticles, and conductive polymers, MXenes’ intrinsic properties, such as high surface area, high electrical conductivity, and tunable surface chemistry, can contribute to improving the sensitivity, selectivity, and stability of PEC biosensors. These characteristics make MXenes suitable for applications across various sectors, such as healthcare, food safety, and environmental monitoring. This review comprehensively outlines the core principles of PEC sensing, highlighting the role of MXene‐based composites and light‐driven processes in facilitating the detection of miRNA, protein biomarkers, small biomolecules, drug molecules, pesticides, and organic contaminants. It further explores recent advancements in MXene composites for detecting a broad spectrum of biological targets in complex biological samples. The review also addresses challenges, including the requirements for stability, reproducibility, biocompatibility, and scalability in various practical applications. Finally, it discusses future perspectives on MXene‐integrated composites for PEC biosensing and their potential applications in clinical diagnostics, precision medicine, food safety, and environmental monitoring.
articles.summary_en: A review examines MXene-integrated composites for photoelectrochemical biosensors targeting biomarkers, biomolecules, drugs, pesticides, and organic contaminants. It highlights potential gains in sensitivity, selectivity, and stability while identifying stability, reproducibility, biocompatibility, and scalability as barriers to deployment.

articles.title_original: The Effect of Mxene on Antibacterial Activity and its Optical Characterization for Biological Application
articles.title_en: MXene nanosheets show enhanced antibacterial activity
articles.excerpt_original: MXene was synthesized from the Ti₃AlC₂ MAX phase via hydrothermal wet chemical etching using a hydrofluoric acid–hydrochloric acid mixture. X ray diffraction showed a shift of the (002) peak to lower 2θ values, indicating expanded interlayer spacing after selective removal of aluminium and surface termination. Scanning electron microscopy revealed the characteristic accordion like, multilayer morphology of exfoliated MXene, while energy dispersive X ray spectroscopy confirmed aluminium depletion and the presence of –F, –O, and –OH terminations. Raman and UV–visible–near infrared spectroscopy verified retained structural integrity and strong broadband optical absorption of the delaminated nanosheets. These observations demonstrate successful etching and exfoliation into high quality, stable Ti₃C₂Tₓ nanosheets with well defined structural and surface characteristics. Antibacterial testing showed improvement for MXene versus MAX. Ti₃AlC₂ gave 14 mm inhibition, ~58% of Nitrofurantoin’s 24 mm. Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene yielded 26 mm, ~8% above the antibiotic and 85% higher than Ti₃AlC₂. Efficacy is attributed to higher surface reactivity and sharper nanosheet edges improving membrane interaction. Thus, Ti₃C₂Tₓ combines optical robustness and superior antibacterial performance, promising for antimicrobial coatings and biomedical environmental applications. The study adds to growing evidence that MXenes, with mechanisms involving physical damage and oxidative stress, can serve as effective antimicrobial agents.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized and characterized Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene nanosheets, observing stronger antibacterial performance than the Ti₃AlC₂ precursor. articles.title_original: Nonlinear Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons at van der Waals topological interfaces
articles.title_en: Nonlinear exciton-polaritons demonstrated at van der Waals topological interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Topological photonic structures provide a powerful means of confining and directing light through interface states formed between photonic phases with distinct topological properties. Van der Waals (vdW) materials offer complementary opportunities for nanophotonics: their optical properties can be selected from a wide family of layered crystals, while their atomically smooth surfaces and lack of lattice-matching constraints enable complex photonic heterostructures to be assembled layer by layer. This flexibility allows topological photonic confinement and strong excitonic coupling to be engineered separately within the same structure. Here, patterned low-loss dielectric hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) defines the photonic modes, while an encapsulated WSe2 monolayer provides the excitonic resonance that couples directly to the confined optical field. We use this approach to realise Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons in a one-dimensional hBN double-grating heterostructure. Strong coupling between the WSe2 exciton and a photonic Jackiw-Rebbi state localised at the interface between two topologically distinct gratings produces upper and lower Jackiw-Rebbi polariton branches. By varying the temperature from 4.7 to 300 K, we tune the exciton across the photonic bandgap and trace the evolution and anticrossing of these branches using angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy. Power-dependent photoluminescence further reveals a pronounced nonlinear response of the confined Jackiw-Rebbi polariton, including a blueshift of up to 5 meV and correlated changes in its intensity scaling and linewidth. These results establish vdW photonic heterostructures as a versatile platform for engineering tunable and nonlinear polaritons localised at topological interfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered Jackiw–Rebbi exciton-polaritons using patterned hexagonal boron nitride and a WSe2 monolayer. Temperature- and power-dependent measurements showed tunable anticrossing and nonlinear behavior, including a blueshift of up to 5 meV, highlighting a platform for tunable topological photonics.

articles.title_original: A nanocomposite-mediated synergistic division inhibition strategy for selective antibacterial therapy against burn infections
articles.title_en: Boron Nitride Nanocomposite Shows Selective Antibacterial Activity in Burn-Infection Models
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nanomaterial-based antibacterial therapy presents an alternative solution to antibiotic resistance. However, most research focuses on enhancing antibacterial activity while neglecting the selectivity of nanomaterials, leading to indiscriminate damage to mammalian cells. Here, we design a synergistic boron nitride-polydopamine@MOF-199 nanocomposite (BPM NC) that interferes with bacterial binary fission. Its selectivity stems from suppressing FtsZ polymerization during bacterial division, while its high efficiency arises from synergistic mechanisms such as disrupting membrane potential and bacterial defense systems. These effects induce molecular-level disruptions in bacterial biological processes, enabling BPM NC (0.35 μg/mL) to rapidly inactivate bacteria (10 7 CFU/mL) in 30 min—358-fold enhancement over its precursor h-BN. In burn infection models, BPM NC exhibits significant efficacy in male mice and female pigs, outperforming the clinical drug silver sulfadiazine. This work provides a promising insight into developing antibacterial nanomaterials that combine selectivity and high activity, offering a strategy for next-generation antibacterial therapies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a boron nitride–polydopamine@MOF-199 nanocomposite that selectively inhibits bacterial division while disrupting membrane potential and defense systems. The material rapidly inactivated bacteria and outperformed silver sulfadiazine in mouse and pig burn-infection models, indicating potential for next-generation antibacterial therapy.

articles.title_original: High luminescence efficiency of multivalley excitonic complexes in heavily doped WSe 2 monolayer
articles.title_en: Heavily Doped WSe₂ Monolayers Deliver Over 50% Quantum Yield
articles.excerpt_original: Monolayers of group-VI transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are two-dimensional semiconductors that exhibit exceptionally strong light-matter coupling yet typically suffer from low emission quantum yields. In this letter, we investigate the heavily n-doped regime of a WSe$_2$ monolayer and show that multi-particle excitonic complexes produce photoluminescence signals up to two orders of magnitude stronger than in the neutral state. Time-resolved photoluminescence and differential reflectivity measurements reveal that the quantum yield rises with carrier density and exceeds 50% for electron concentrations above 10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. These findings establish TMD monolayers as a platform for exploring excitonic complexes in high-density electron gases and point toward new opportunities for efficient, atomically thin light emitters.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that multivalley excitonic complexes increase photoluminescence in heavily n-doped WSe₂ monolayers by up to two orders of magnitude. articles.title_original: Edge Chemical Passivation Engineering of Armchair MoSi 2 N 4 Nanoribbon PMOS Field‐Effect Transistors: A First‐Principles DFT–NEGF Investigation
articles.title_en: DFT Study Shows Fluorine Passivation Improves MoSi₂N₄ Nanoribbon PMOS Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Edge chemical passivation provides an effective strategy for tuning the electronic and transport properties of two‐dimensional semiconductor nanoribbons. Here, the effects of hydrogen (H), chlorine (Cl), and fluorine (F) edge passivation on armchair MoSi 2 N 4 nanoribbon PMOS field‐effect transistors are systematically investigated using density functional theory combined with the nonequilibrium Green’s function (DFT–NEGF) approach. The electronic band structure, density of states (DOS), transmission spectrum, transfer characteristics, and transconductance are analyzed to elucidate the impact of edge termination. All passivation configurations improve the electronic and transport characteristics relative to the pristine nanoribbon. The electronic bandgap increases from 1.80 eV for the pristine structure to 1.88, 1.95, and 2.03 eV for H‐, Cl‐, and F‐passivated structures, respectively, while the DOS gap increases from 1.16 to 1.34, 1.38, and 1.56 eV. These changes indicate effective suppression of localized edge states. Among the investigated configurations, F passivation yields the highest ON‐state current and I ON / I OFF ratio, while maintaining a comparable OFF‐state current. The enhanced performance is attributed to the high electronegativity of F, which promotes edge charge redistribution and carrier confinement.
articles.summary_en: A first-principles DFT–NEGF study finds that hydrogen, chlorine, and fluorine edge passivation improves the electronic and transport characteristics of armchair MoSi₂N₄ nanoribbon PMOS transistors. Fluorine delivers the highest ON-state current and ON/OFF ratio by suppressing localized edge states and promoting carrier confinement.

articles.title_original: Growth and morphology of core-shell nanowires incorporating dissimilar hexagonal semiconductors: the case of InAs-ZnTe
articles.title_en: Defect-Free InAs–ZnTe Core–Shell Nanowires Grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy
articles.excerpt_original: Core-shell nanowires incorporating semiconductors from two groups, III-V for the core and II-VI for the shell, have been grown by molecular beam epitaxy in two dedicated chambers connected under ultra-high vacuum, and studied by electron microscopy. During the growth of the shell, the wurtzite structure of the core is replicated in the shell, without any creation of defects. This is true for a wide range of shell thickness, from about one monolayer, up to 25 nm thanks to the good lattice match between the InAs material of the core and the ZnTe material of the shell. While (1 100) m-facets and (11 20) a-facets coexist on the sidewalls of the core, during the growth of the ZnTe shell the size of the m-facets progressively increases at the expense of the a-facets which eventually disappear. A fast growth of the ZnTe shell is observed for the first few monolayers, with a high sticking; this is followed by a slower growth, of the same order of magnitude as observed on a ZnTe core, with a dependence on the nanowire radius which points to the occurrence of mononuclear nucleation
articles.summary_en: Researchers grew InAs–ZnTe core–shell nanowires with defect-free transfer of the core’s wurtzite structure across shell thicknesses up to 25 nm. The study identifies facet evolution and radius-dependent nucleation behavior relevant to engineering semiconductor nanowire heterostructures.

articles.title_original: Ammonium thiocyanate enables in-situ structural templating of MAPbI3 via quasi-2D perovskite scaffold
articles.title_en: Ammonium thiocyanate templates MAPbI3 perovskite growth
articles.excerpt_original: Ammonium thiocyanate (NH4SCN) has been used extensively to improve the current extraction and device performance of quasi-two-dimensional perovskite solar cells. Whilst this additive has been shown to influence quasi-2D perovskite crystallisation, a detailed understanding of its mechanism has not yet been established. Through spectroscopic and structural studies, we demonstrate that NH4SCN enables quasi-2D perovskite phases to structurally template the dominant 3D phase. Contrary to previous reports, we suggest that the benefit of this additive comes from an improvement to the 3D perovskite structure, not from charges transferring through vertically oriented 2D perovskite layers. We show that this additive provides kinetic control over the quasi-2D phase formation, suppressing the unfavourable n = 1 perovskite phase and promoting the growth of high-n 2D scaffold phases by extending the nucleation window. This promotes the in-situ templated growth of MAPbI3. We provide robust structural analysis demonstrating highly (110)-ordered 3D perovskite, with the mechanism confirmed by close lattice matching between this phase and quasi-2D phases. Furthermore, we show that this structural control is cation dependent, requiring both close lattice matching between quasi-2D and 3D perovskite phases, and successful kinetic control of the relevant quasi-2D phases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that ammonium thiocyanate improves MAPbI3 formation by kinetically suppressing unfavorable n=1 quasi-2D phases and promoting high-n scaffold phases. The findings attribute performance gains to improved 3D perovskite structure rather than charge transfer through vertically oriented 2D layers.

articles.title_original: Data-Driven Analysis of C–F Bond Lengths in Two-Dimensional Fluorinated Carbon Materials
articles.title_en: Data-Driven Analysis of C–F Bonds in Fluorinated Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The C–F bond length is an important structural descriptor of fluorinated carbon materials, but its reported values remain widely scattered across the literature. Here, a compilation and statistical analysis of C–F bond lengths is presented, focusing on two-dimensional (2D) fluorinated carbon materials and comparing them with fluorinated low-dimensional and molecular systems. The 2D dataset comprises 176 entries spanning C0.86F to C200F and covering publications from 1934 to 2026. It includes bulk, single-layer, and double-layer architectures, with carbon conformation in bulk structures also taken into account (e.g., puckered, planar, and mixed sp2/sp3). Mean C–F bond lengths decrease progressively from bulk graphite fluorides and fluorine–graphite intercalation compounds (~1.42 Å) to single- and double-layer fluorographenes (~1.40 and ~1.38 Å, respectively). They are generally longer than those of conventional molecular fluorides, fluorocarbonium ions and fluorocarbenium ions, but shorter than those in three-center fluoronium ions. Experimental determinations from the literature, including solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance and X-ray/neutron pair distribution function analysis, give broadly consistent mean bond lengths. Computational results from the literature likewise show broadly consistent values across exchange–correlation functionals. Decreasing fluorine content increases the mean C–F bond length by ~9% from ~1.39 Å for CF to ~1.51 Å for C16F. Puckeredchair structures generally show longer C–F bonds than puckered-boat structures, with a difference of ~0.04 Å in bulk materials. Together, these results provide an accessible reference that brings scattered C–F bond-length data together, revealing statistically supported trends that are difficult to identify from
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers statistically analyzed 176 reported C–F bond lengths in two-dimensional fluorinated carbon materials. The study identifies trends linked to fluorine content, layer structure, and carbon conformation, providing a reference for fluorographene research.

articles.title_original: Quantum Monte-Carlo study of spin-valley ferromagnetism in rhombohedral graphene
articles.title_en: Quantum Monte Carlo reveals low-temperature ferromagnetism in rhombohedral graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Recent capacitance measurements in bilayer and trilayer rhombohedral graphene reported large magnetic entropy above the Curie temperature, suggesting the formation of fluctuating local moments. Further experimental support comes from scanning tunneling microscopy experiments in rhombohedral hexalayer graphene, which directly visualized honeycomb electron-crystal order that strengthens upon heating before melting, related to the Pomeranchuk effect. Motivated by these experiments, we construct spin-valley local-moment Hamiltonians for the quarter-metal and half-metal phases. We extract their couplings from constrained Hartree-Fock calculations, and solve their finite-temperature thermodynamics with stochastic-series-expansion quantum Monte Carlo. For the quarter metal we find a continuous 2D-Ising transition at $T_c \approx 0.7$ K, an order of magnitude smaller than the Hartree-Fock estimate (~30 K) and closer to the experimental scale of a few kelvin. For the half metal, we study the field-induced magnetization as a function of temperature with and without proximity-enhanced spin-orbit coupling. When spin-orbit coupling is negligible, intervalley Hund's coupling enhances the magnetic response. Strong spin-orbit coupling, as can be induced by a neighboring transition-metal dichalcogenide, gives rise to the standard spin-canted ground state at zero temperature. Upon heating, the in-plane polarization decreases more rapidly than the out-of-plane polarization. Surprisingly, despite the itinerant nature of the electrons, local-moment models with microscopically determined couplings appear to capture key finite-temperature magnetic properties of rhombohedral graphene without any fitting.
articles.summary_en: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations predict a two-dimensional Ising transition near 0.7 K in quarter-metal rhombohedral graphene, substantially below Hartree–Fock estimates and closer to experimental temperatures. The results indicate that local-moment models can capture finite-temperature magnetic behavior, including spin–orbit-coupling effects in half-metal phases.

articles.title_original: Coexistence of Superconductivity and Chern insulators with |C| $\geq 1$ in twisted rhombohedral bilayer-trilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Twisted rhombohedral graphene shows coexisting superconductivity and Chern insulators
articles.excerpt_original: Rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) has been demonstrated as a promising platform for investigating strongly correlated phases of matter. Here, we observe a coexistence of superconductivity and Chern insulators in a twisted rhombohedral bilayer-trilayer graphene moiré superlattice. Superconductivity, evidenced by a sharp transition with a critical temperature of ~180 mK, nonlinear I-V with a BKT temperature of 135 mK, and a signature of phase-sensitive interference patterns, emerges from a symmetry-breaking Fermi surface near v = -2 and D = 0, and it survives at a large in-plane magnetic field up to 2 T, strongly deviating from the Pauli limit. Moreover, we observe a strong modulation of the Ginzburg-Landau coherence length from 467 nm to 145 nm as the in-plane magnetic field increases from 0 to 2 T, whereas the critical current Ic barely changes. Unlike previous studies in RMG, we observe a competition between superconductivity and a correlated insulator at v = -2, monitored by displacement fields and twist angles. Note that we also observe integer Chern insulators with C = 1, 3, and -3 at v = 1/2, 1, and 3, respectively, for large D > 0 in the same superconducting device. The observations establish twisted rhombohedral graphene multilayers as a fascinating system to investigate unconventional superconductivity, high Chern number topology, and their interplay.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report superconductivity and integer Chern insulators in twisted rhombohedral bilayer–trilayer graphene. The device exhibits a critical temperature of about 180 mK, survives in-plane fields up to 2 T, and shows Chern numbers of 1, 3, and −3, highlighting a platform for studying unconventional superconductivity and topology.

articles.title_original: Co--dsorption of terrylene and tetrapentacontane on hexagonal boron nitride - towards a two-dimensional Shpolskii matrix
articles.title_en: hBN Host–Guest Matrix Stabilizes Single-Molecule Emitters
articles.excerpt_original: Organic molecular emitters are promising building blocks for quantum technologies, but their use at two-dimensional interfaces is limited by diffusion, aggregation, and photobleaching. We present work towards constructing an ultrathin two-dimensional Shpolskii-like host-guest matrix on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) by co-depositing terrylene fluorophores with the long-chain tetrapentacontane in a solution-phase process. We demonstrate that this approach disperses terrylene in a roughly one-nanometer-thin alkane layer without detectable phase separation and allows tuning the emitter density from ensembles to isolated emitters showing characteristic blinking behavior consistent with single-molecule fluorescence. Time-lapse confocal microscopy, autocorrelation analysis, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching show that suppressed diffusion and stable emitter positions can be achieved in several samples with a tetrapentacontane matrix. Encapsulation with hBN from the top side further improves photostability, with emitters demonstrating long lifetimes despite high photon doses. Successful co-adsorption of isolated emitters and alkane matrix is a milestone towards extending Shpolskii-type molecular isolation to hBN and provides a route towards stable, interface-integrated molecular qubits.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a roughly one-nanometer-thick tetrapentacontane matrix on hexagonal boron nitride that disperses terrylene emitters from ensembles to isolated molecules. The approach suppresses diffusion and improves photostability, supporting potential interface-integrated molecular qubits.

articles.title_original: Geometry-dependent crack interaction and toughening in graphene
articles.title_en: Graphene Crack Geometry Influences Toughness and Fracture Behavior
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The interaction between neighboring cracks has been shown to strongly influence the fracture behavior of graphene. While previous studies focused primarily on crack spacing, the role of crack width remains poorly understood. Here, computational simulations are performed to investigate the coupled effects of crack width and inter-crack spacing $$(W_\text {gap})$$ ( W gap ) on the tensile response of graphene containing parallel cracks. The results show that increasing crack width amplifies the sensitivity of mechanical properties to crack spacing, leading to significant enhancement of peak stress, fracture strain, and toughness at sufficiently large $$W_\text {gap}$$ W gap . For narrow cracks, crack coalescence dominates and causes brittle failure. In contrast, wider cracks promote delayed ligament rupture and increased energy absorption, which are referred to as ductile-like fracture behavior. The normalized toughness and fracture strain exceed those of equivalent single-crack systems by more than twofold. A heat-map summarizes how peak stress and toughness change with crack width, spacing, and chirality.
articles.summary_en: Computational simulations show that crack width and spacing jointly govern graphene’s tensile response. Wider cracks can delay ligament rupture and more than double normalized toughness and fracture strain compared with equivalent single-crack systems, while narrow cracks promote brittle coalescence.

articles.title_original: Observation of light-induced topological state in graphene
articles.title_en: Light-induced topological state observed in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Driving quantum materials with light can reshape not only their electronic band structures but also the geometry of their electronic wavefunctions. In graphene, circularly polarized light is predicted to open gaps at the Dirac points and induce a pseudospin texture and Berry curvature characteristic of the Haldane model, realizing a Floquet Chern insulator. Transport and all-optical measurements have provided evidence for a light-induced anomalous Hall response, but cannot resolve the underlying electronic states in both energy and momentum space. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy has revealed Floquet-Bloch sidebands and hybridization gaps at crossings between Floquet bands. However, these experiments used linearly polarized driving, which preserves time-reversal symmetry and thus does not induce a topological phase. Here, we combine circular-dichroic time-resolved extreme-ultraviolet momentum microscopy with ab initio theory to investigate graphene driven by circularly polarized light. We observe a pump-induced photoemission circular dichroism near the Dirac point that reverses sign with pump helicity and across the Dirac energy, in agreement with our calculations. These results link the measured dichroic response to the light-induced pseudospin texture and its associated Berry curvature, providing spectroscopic evidence for the Floquet-engineered topological insulating state in graphene.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used circular-dichroic time-resolved extreme-ultraviolet momentum microscopy and ab initio theory to observe a light-induced pseudospin texture and Berry curvature in graphene. The findings provide spectroscopic evidence for a Floquet-engineered topological insulating state, with potential relevance to optically controlled quantum and electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Electrochemical functionalization of graphene rationalized by Hammett and Swain-Lupton parameters
articles.title_en: Electrochemical Functionalization Enables Stable, Tunable Graphene Conductance
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene's sp^{2}-bonded carbon lattice makes it exceptionally resistant to covalent functionalization, with existing approaches relying on chemically specific and often harsh methods, fragmenting our understanding of its reactivity. Here we show that electric fields of approximately 1 V nm^{-1} in non-aqueous electrolytes enable the electrochemical functionalization of monolayer graphene with a broad range of substituents, leading to two-order-of-magnitude conductance modulation stable over 5,000 cycles and semi-reversible electronic conductor-insulator transitions. Analysis of the oxidation potentials across substituents reveals trends governed by classical descriptors. Species forming localised σ bonds display increasing oxidation potentials with the meta-Hammett constant (σ_m), whereas substituents interacting via delocalised π orbitals follow an inverse dependence on the modified Swain-Lupton resonance parameter (R). These relationships indicate that graphene's oxidation potential increases with the electron-withdrawing strength of the substituent. Our results provide new insights into the electrochemical activity of inert materials under strong electric fields.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that strong electric fields in non-aqueous electrolytes can functionalize monolayer graphene with diverse substituents, producing stable conductance modulation over 5,000 cycles. Hammett and Swain–Lupton analyses link oxidation potential to substituent electronic effects, offering a framework for tuning graphene’s electronic behavior.

articles.title_original: Moiré-enabled chiral plasmons in twisted bilayer graphene nanoislands
articles.title_en: Twisted bilayer graphene nanoislands enable tunable chiral plasmons
articles.excerpt_original: Twisting two stacked graphene layers superimposes a moiré superlattice that reshapes their electronic structure, yet how it shapes the collective optical response of finite, nanoscale bilayers remains largely unexplored. Using an atomistic tight-binding and self-consistent density-matrix approach, we compute the twist-dependent plasmonic response of twisted bilayer graphene nanoislands comprising thousands of atoms. The spectra are strongly tunable and split into two regimes at a critical angle where a single moiré wavelength spans the island; beyond it, an ordered ladder of resonances emerges whenever an integer number of moiré periods fits within the overlapping bilayer. In doped islands, the interlayer coupling also produces a moiré-enabled Born--Kuhn chiral plasmon: opposite transverse dipoles in the two layers form an electric quadrupole that hybridizes with the bright dipole, opening an anticrossing near the critical angle, with a handedness that reverses with the twist direction. Triangular islands confirm that the moiré lattice, not the flake boundary, governs both effects, establishing twist as a mechanical handle on chiral graphene plasmons.
articles.summary_en: A theoretical study finds that twist angle and moiré periodicity strongly tune plasmon resonances in finite twisted bilayer graphene nanoislands. Interlayer coupling can generate chiral plasmons whose handedness reverses with twist direction, suggesting a mechanical route to controllable nanoscale optical responses.

articles.title_original: Mie Scattering-Enhanced Fluorinated Polyether Ether Ketone Nanofibrous Films for Efficient Radiative Heat Dissipation
articles.title_en: Fluorinated PEEK Nanofiber Film Enables High-Performance Radiative Cooling
articles.excerpt_original: This study develops a high-performance radiative cooling (RC) composite film based on electrospinning fluorinated polyether ether ketone, incorporating titanium dioxide (TiO2) and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) as functional fillers to achieve exceptional spectral selectivity with a solar reflectance of 96.51% and mid-infrared emissivity of 95.12%. The three-dimensional porous fibrous network endows the film with outstanding RC performance, achieving a maximum sub-ambient temperature reduction of 14.63 °C under direct sunlight and a temperature reduction of 8.66 °C relative to the bare vehicle model in small-scale outdoor vehicle tests, thereby validating the significant cooling advantage of the electrospinning film under real-world service conditions. The synergistic effect of the porous fibrous network and intrinsically low-surface-energy matrix imparts self-cleaning functionality to the film (water contact angle of 151.46° and sliding angle of approximately 5°), while solar reflectance degradation remains below 3% after the aging test, demonstrating long-term outdoor service reliability. EnergyPlus building energy simulations confirmed that the film achieved annual energy savings exceeding 6% in tropical arid cities, with positive net energy savings across the vast majority of global climate regions. This film provides a comprehensive design paradigm for high-performance multifunctional RC materials, with broad application prospects for low-carbon building energy conservation and outdoor thermal management.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a fluorinated PEEK nanofibrous composite film with TiO₂ and hexagonal boron nitride fillers, achieving 96.51% solar reflectance and 95.12% mid-infrared emissivity. The self-cleaning film reduced temperatures by up to 14.63°C and delivered simulated annual building energy savings above 6% in tropical arid climates, indicating potential for outdoor thermal management and energy-efficient construction.

articles.title_original: Enhanced performance of hydrogen-terminated diamond FETs via two-photon UV laser etching
articles.title_en: UV laser etching boosts hydrogen-terminated diamond FET performance sixfold
articles.excerpt_original: Hydrogen-terminated diamond field-effect transistors (FETs) have attracted interest for high-power and high-frequency electronics. However, their performance remains limited by high surface resistance and fabrication complexity. Two-photon UV laser etching is a direct method for enhancing the surface conductivity. In this work, we investigate effect of UV etching on the active region of hydrogen-terminated diamond FETs. Devices fabricated on laser-etched surfaces show up to a sixfold increase in drain current density, reaching 0.22 A/mm compared with 0.035 A/mm for devices fabricated on unprocessed surfaces. The enhancement is largely removed by subsequent oxygen plasma treatment, indicating that the improvement originates from the laser-modified near-surface region. Additionally, the UV laser processing facilitates in situ isolation of conductive regions, simplifying fabrication. These findings highlight UV laser etching as a scalable and effective technique for enhancing diamond-based electronics.
articles.summary_en: Academic research reports that two-photon UV laser etching increased drain current density in hydrogen-terminated diamond FETs from 0.035 to 0.22 A/mm. The process also enables in situ isolation of conductive regions, potentially simplifying scalable fabrication of high-power and high-frequency diamond electronics.

articles.title_original: Precise Sputter Control by Tailored Waveform Biasing for Selective Ablation in Future 2D Electronics Manufacturing
articles.title_en: Tailored Plasma Waveforms Enable Selective Etching for 2D Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Precise control of ion energy in plasma processes is pivotal for the selective, damage‐free etching that future two‐dimensional (2D) electronics demand. Conventional equipment technology with RF sinusoidal waveform biasing is unable to generate the monoenergetic ion energy distribution function (IEDF) required for the selective sputtering of materials that exhibit only marginal differences in threshold ion energy for sputtering. Applying a low‐frequency tailored pulse‐wave‐shaped bias voltage waveform to the substrate electrode of a commercial 200 mm inductively coupled plasma (ICP) plasma reactor results in an IEDF with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of just 10 eV even at higher ion energies. These narrow IEDFs are used within this study to determine the sputtering thresholds of molybdenum disulfide () and selected dielectrics: , , and , with the aim of enabling the efficient selective physical etching of dielectric materials relative to 2D materials, and vice versa. Armed with this knowledge, the dielectric environment and layer structure can be designed specifically to the application at hand, ensuring the highest possible selectivity in the patterning process. Additionally, a tailored waveform bias allows layers of varying quality to be plasma cleaned below the sputtering threshold energy.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated low-frequency tailored bias waveforms that narrow ion-energy distributions to about 10 eV in a 200 mm plasma reactor. The approach enables selective sputtering of MoS₂ and dielectric materials, potentially improving damage-free patterning and plasma cleaning in future 2D electronics manufacturing.

articles.title_original: Giant Magneto-Photoresponse in 2D Room-Temperature Magnetic Semiconductor Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Large-Scale 2D Magnetic Heterostructures Enable Room-Temperature Magneto-Photoresponse
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) magnetic semiconductor heterostructures serve as an ideal material platform for the exploration of emergent physical phenomena and high-density integrated electronics, owing to the strong magneto-electric-optical coupling at their interfaces. Remarkably, the interfacial engineering also endows the heterosystem with pronounced multifield tunability, facilitating the development of next-generation low-power multifunctional devices. Nevertheless, their practical development remains hindered by low magnetic ordering temperatures and the lack of scalable synthetic methods. Here, we develop a dual precursor-assisted chemical vapor deposition strategy to achieve large-scale synthesis of room-temperature-operable FeSex/WSe2 magnetic semiconductor heterostructures with atomically sharp interfaces. The photoresponse of the as-fabricated heterostructure can be effectively programmed by an external magnetic field, achieving a prominent room-temperature modulation ratio exceeding 50%. Such impressive magneto-photoresponse originates from spin-dependent interfacial charge transfer. Furthermore, the synergistic tunability of photoelectric performance under varying illumination and magnetic fields facilitates the construction of an adaptive enhancement framework for magnetic sensing, which enables optimized low-contrast image recognition and paves the way for advanced in-sensor computing systems. This work not only provides a feasible synthetic route for large-scale preparation of 2D heterostructures, but also sheds new light on the design of multifunctional devices with multifield coupling characteristics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a dual-precursor CVD method for atomically sharp FeSex/WSe2 heterostructures that operate at room temperature and show magnetic-field-controlled photoresponse modulation above 50%. The platform supports adaptive magnetic sensing, low-contrast image recognition, and potential in-sensor computing, although practical scale-up remains an important consideration.

articles.title_original: Continuous Semiconductor-to-Half-Metal-to-Metal Transition in 1D/2D CuX2/CrBr3 Heterostructures via Anion Substitution and Interfacial Compression
articles.title_en: CuX₂/CrBr₃ Heterostructures Enable Tunable Half-Metallicity
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate one-dimensional (1D) CuBr2 and CuCl2 chains and their mixed-dimensional heterostructures with two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic CrBr3, focusing on the interfacial coupling mechanism and the continuous electronic transition behavior. Both heterostructures form stable stacking configurations with preserved ferromagnetic ground states. By interfacial compression, the CuBr2/CrBr3 heterostructure undergoes a continuous semiconductor-to-half-metal-to-metal transition. Remarkably, the half-metallic state emerges within a narrow window between approximately 2.78 and 2.85 Å, while the CuCl2/CrBr3 heterostructure remains semiconducting under all compression strains. Charge density difference and projected band structure analyses reveal that compression enhances the Br-p and Cu-d orbital hybridization at the CuBr2/CrBr3 interface, pushing the Br-p-dominated spin-up valence band maximum across the Fermi level and closing the spin-up gap. For CuCl2/CrBr3, the Cl-p orbitals lie farther from the Fermi level due to Cl’s higher electronegativity, preventing gap closure. This work establishes halogen species as a key control parameter for interfacial half-metallicity, providing a design principle for engineering half-metallicity in mixed-dimensional heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that compressing CuBr₂/CrBr₃ heterostructures drives a continuous semiconductor-to-half-metal-to-metal transition, while CuCl₂/CrBr₃ remains semiconducting. The results identify halogen chemistry and interfacial compression as design parameters for engineering spin-polarized electronic states.

articles.title_original: Cu2MoS4 nanosheet/Silicon (2D/3D) vertical heterojunction for an efficient UV–Vis-NIR photodetection
articles.title_en: Cu₂MoS₄–Silicon Heterojunction Enables UV–Vis–NIR Photodetection
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a vertical 2D/3D heterojunction combining Cu₂MoS₄ nanosheets with silicon for photodetection across the ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared spectrum. The work indicates potential for broad-spectrum semiconductor sensing, although performance details are not provided in the source excerpt.

articles.title_original: Graphene Josephson diodes from asymmetric disorder
articles.title_en: Graphene Josephson diodes achieve over 20% supercurrent rectification
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Josephson diodes are non-reciprocal superconducting devices characterized by different switching currents depending on the current flow direction. They recently attracted considerable theoretical and experimental attention, in view of their possible application as rectifying elements in the field of superconducting electronics, and as probes to investigate symmetry breaking mechanisms in mesoscopic systems. In this work, we show that graphene Josephson junctions provide rectification of supercurrent with an efficiency exceeding 20 % . The effect appears applying a mT out-of-plane magnetic field and is enhanced close to the nodes of the Fraunhofer interference pattern. Our findings are consistent with a theoretical model that considers long-range scattering potentials in the junction as the symmetry-breaking mechanism, which yields supercurrent rectification in highly transparent junctions. While graphene stands out as an ultra-clean transmission medium, our work shows that unavoidable residual disorder is sufficient to promote this effect.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report graphene Josephson junctions with supercurrent rectification efficiency exceeding 20% under a millitesla out-of-plane magnetic field. The findings show that residual disorder can induce diode behavior, supporting potential use in superconducting electronics and studies of symmetry breaking.

articles.title_original: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials
articles.title_en: ML-COHP Accelerates Bond-Strength Prediction for Graphene-Supported Nanoparticles
articles.excerpt_original: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a machine-learning model that predicts integrated crystal orbital Hamilton populations from universal interatomic-potential descriptors, reducing computational time from hours to about one second in tested systems. Applications included Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed oxygen, where the model reproduced bonding trends with low error.

articles.title_original: Odd-Even Parity of Nonlinear Hall Effects in Bilayer Graphene - APS Journals
articles.title_en: Odd–Even Parity of Nonlinear Hall Effects in Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Odd-Even Parity of Nonlinear Hall Effects in Bilayer Graphene APS Journals
articles.summary_en: Researchers report on the parity of nonlinear Hall effects in bilayer graphene. The work advances understanding of graphene’s electronic transport phenomena, with potential relevance to semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: Graphene Islands as a Platform for Band-Structure Engineering
articles.title_en: Graphene Islands Offer Tunable Band-Structure Engineering
articles.excerpt_original: Multilayer graphenes have emerged as a versatile avenue towards exploring novel electronic phases of matter. Recently, nanoscale multilayer graphene islands have been realized experimentally, where the island is less than 50 nm in diameter and distinct in layer configuration from the contact portion of the same graphene sheets, the latter of which act as leads for transport probes. Here, we theoretically investigate how the proximity between these islands and their chemically identical environment modifies the electronic structure. Within the tight-binding approximation, we find that the proximity effect is enhanced by the closely matched momenta between both parts, creating an unusually strong band renormalization which persists as the island size is increased, and only limited by the coherence length. An effective single-unit-cell Hamiltonian to capture these modifications is derived, expressed in terms of interlayer hopping parameters that scale with the relative island area. We predict a substantially altered low-energy density of states for 3- and 4-layer graphene islands, demonstrating the tunability of the electronic structure by spatial size.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical modelling shows that nanoscale multilayer graphene islands can strongly modify low-energy electronic states through proximity effects with adjacent graphene regions. The predicted size-dependent electronic tunability could support future electronic and semiconductor device research.

articles.title_original: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
articles.title_en: Machine learning accelerates discovery and synthesis of new MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning-assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth-based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used machine-learning database mining to identify 33 previously unrecognized MXene candidates and synthesized seven through a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature process. They also produced 11 rare-earth-based MXenes, expanding the material family and revealing potentially diverse semiconducting and magnetic behavior.

articles.title_original: Density functional prediction of 2D spintronic materials: magnetic doping of semiconducting 1T-GeO 2 monolayer
articles.title_en: DFT predicts transition-metal-doped GeO₂ monolayers for spintronics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The search of new two-dimensional (2D) materials, for practical usage in the emergent field of spintronics, is a very active topic due to the exceptional properties of these systems compared to their corresponding bulk phases. In the present study, we use DFT calculations to investigate the electronic structure and magnetic ordering of 1T-GeO 2 monolayer, doped with transition metal (TM) elements: V, Cr, and Mn; at 25\% doping concentration. The undoped monolayer is predicted to be an ultrawide band gap semiconductor (with 5.34 ~ eV indirect band gap). When the ferromagnetic ordering is considered, the V-doped system is found to be a half-metal; while the Cr- and Mn-doped ones exhibit a semiconducting character. The mechanism responsible for these predicted features is also examined. This suggests that transition metal-doped 1T-GeO 2 could be advantageous for spintronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Density functional theory predicts that semiconducting 1T-GeO₂ monolayers doped with vanadium, chromium, or manganese exhibit altered electronic and magnetic properties. Vanadium doping produces a predicted half-metallic state, while chromium and manganese doping remain semiconducting, indicating potential use in spintronic devices.

articles.title_original: Exceptional Superconducting Interfaces between Graphene and Atomic Chains in A15-MoRe
articles.title_en: Graphene–MoRe Interfaces Reveal A15 Superconducting Origin of Robust Quantum Contacts
articles.excerpt_original: Realizing highly transparent and magnetic-field-resilient superconducting contacts is a critical bottleneck for the advancement of two-dimensional (2D) quantum devices. Molybdenum-rhenium (MoRe) alloys have been empirically favored as they uniquely yield ballistic, highly transparent contacts to graphene that survive in high-magnetic-field regimes; however, the microscopic origin of this anomalous transparency has remained a long-standing puzzle. Here, we resolve this paradox by revealing that pristine graphene/MoRe interfaces are governed by the classical A15 superconducting phase. Combining low-temperature transport, X-ray diffraction, and atomic-resolution electron microscopy, we demonstrate that as-deposited MoRe spontaneously forms the A15 phase in direct contact with graphene, whereas thermal annealing triggers a phase transition to a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure that severely degrades the Josephson transparency. Crucially, the one-dimensional (1D) transition-metal atomic chains unique to the A15 structure exhibit a near-perfect lattice match (mismatch < 1%) with graphene edges. First-principles calculations further prove that the d-orbitals of these historically renowned 1D chains possibly hybridize with graphene's Dirac cone near the K point. These findings not only uncover the structural and electronic origins of optimal MoRe contacts but also establish A15-phase superconductors as a geometrically ideal, universal platform for realizing robust quantum electronics based on 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that as-deposited MoRe forms an A15 superconducting phase directly at graphene interfaces, enabling highly transparent, magnetic-field-resilient contacts. Annealing converts MoRe to an hcp phase and severely reduces Josephson transparency, highlighting a potential materials-design route for graphene-based quantum electronics.

articles.title_original: MXene‐Based Hybrid Photodetectors: A Review of Multidimensional Material Integration (0D, 1D, and 2D)
articles.title_en: Review outlines MXene hybrid photodetector design strategies
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXenes, an emerging family of two‐dimensional transition‐metal carbides and nitrides, exhibit a distinctive blend of metallic conductivity, adjustable surface chemistry, and strong light–matter interactions, making them highly attractive for optoelectronic applications. However, their intrinsically weak photoresponse and environmental instability limit standalone device performance. Here, we present a critical and unified perspective on MXene‐based hybrid photodetectors enabled by multidimensional integration with zero‐(0D), one‐(1D), and two‐(2D) dimensional materials. We establish a design framework linking dimensionality with interfacial charge‐transfer mechanisms, band alignment, and carrier transport pathways. MXene/0D hybrids achieve ultrahigh photogain via trap‐assisted photogating, whereas MXene/1D architectures enable directional transport and rapid carrier extraction. MXene/2D heterostructures, in contrast, suppress dark current and enhance stability through efficient van der Waals coupling. We further highlight the central role of surface terminations in modulating work function and interfacial energetics. Despite rapid progress, challenges in stability, interface control, and scalable fabrication persist. By correlating materials chemistry with device physics, this review provides actionable design rules and outlines emerging directions, including infrared photodetection, flexible systems, and neuromorphic optoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: A review examines MXene-based photodetectors combined with 0D, 1D and 2D materials to improve photogain, charge transport, dark-current suppression and stability. articles.title_original: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene - Nature
articles.title_en: Attosecond videography captures Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically 1–9 . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion 10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light 12–19 , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta 8,20 . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography to visualize strong-field-driven electron motion and non-adiabatic tunnelling across graphene’s first Brillouin zone. The technique provides new insight into coherent electronic control and scattering in quantum materials.

articles.excerpt_original: The protein corona (PC) that forms on the surface of nanomaterials upon contact with biological fluids provides a molecular snapshot of the host's physiological and pathological state. Here, we investigate two-dimensional (2D) titanium carbide (Ti3C2Tx) MXene nanosheets as nanobiointerfaces for capturing Alzheimer's disease (AD)-associated plasma protein signatures. Ti3C2Tx MXene flakes were incubated with plasma from clinically diagnosed AD patients and age-matched healthy controls (HC), leading to the formation of Ti3C2Tx MXene-PC complexes. Physicochemical characterization using dynamic light scattering, zeta potential analysis, and transmission electron microscopy revealed disease-dependent changes in hydrodynamic size, surface charge, and PC profile. Proteomic analysis of the isolated PC layers quantified 1,611 proteins without prior fractionation, demonstrating broad plasma proteome coverage. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed disease-associated separation between AD and HC-derived Ti3C2Tx MXene PC proteomes along specific principal components despite interindividual heterogeneity. Differential abundance analysis identified selective enrichment of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs), annexins, and inflammatory mediators in AD-derived PC, implicating dysregulated RNA metabolism, membrane stress responses, and immune activation, hallmark processes in AD pathology. Our findings demonstrate that Ti3C2Tx MXene-PC interfaces reshape the detectable plasma proteome and enable disease-associated molecular phenotyping, establishing a versatile nanointerface-driven framework for AD-related proteomic fingerprinting and molecular profiling. These results provide a foundation for future studies exploring MXene-based biointerfaces for plasma biomarker disc
articles.summary_en: Researchers used Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene nanosheets to capture and analyze plasma protein coronas from Alzheimer’s disease patients and healthy controls. The interfaces quantified 1,611 proteins and revealed disease-associated proteomic differences, supporting future MXene-based biomarker profiling.

articles.title_original: Electrically Active Composite Hydrogel Membranes With MXene for Bone Defect Repair
articles.title_en: MXene Composite Hydrogel Membrane Enhances Electrically Stimulated Bone Repair
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Electrical stimulation (ES) is widely acknowledged as an efficient means for enhancing bone repair. Despite the promising results of synergistic techniques that integrate conductive nanomaterials and ES in excitable tissues, their utilization in bone defect repair is yet inadequately investigated, given the inherent bioelectrical characteristics of bone tissue. In this work, a new osteogenic polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/pectin/MXene (Ti 3 C 2 T x ) (PPM) conductive composite hydrogel membrane is designed and comprehensively assessed for its efficacy in electrically enhanced bone regeneration. The PPM membrane with a durable threedimensional (3D) conductive network is formed by combining mechanically resilient, biocompatible PVA and bioactive pectin with highly conductive MXene nanosheets. PVA ensures mechanical integrity and structural stability, pectin with many functional groups promotes cell adhesion and osteogenic bioactivity, while the integration of MXene significantly enhances electrical conductivity, promoting cellular electrical signal transmission and modulating osteogenic cell activities. The PPM membrane has advantageous electrical, mechanical characteristics, and excellent in vitro cytocompatibility and improved osteogenic potential. In vivo experiments indicate that the PPM membrane markedly enhances new bone growth when subjected to ES. This study presents a synergistic approach utilizing a conductive hydrogel membrane and ES, providing a viable biomaterial platform for the repair of bone defects.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a conductive PVA/pectin/MXene hydrogel membrane designed to support bone regeneration under electrical stimulation. articles.title_original: Synergistic structural coupling of MXene and La–Ti–O metal-organic framework for high-energy-density flexible solid-state supercapacitors

articles.excerpt_original: For energy storage applications, the practical potential of single materials is usually limited by their intrinsic drawbacks. Specifically, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) suffer from poor conductivity, while 2D MXenes are prone to oxidation and restacking. Herein, in situ growth of La–Ti–O MOF on Ti3C2Tx MXene is reported to enable synergistic structural coupling of MXene@La–Ti–O composite for high-performance supercapacitors. La–Ti–O MOF is in-situ grown from lanthanum-coordinated titanium-oxo cluster precursors on MXene nanosheets, and the synergistic structural coupling of MXene@La–Ti–O can effectively inhibit the restacking of MXene nanosheets, enrich redox active sites, and simultaneously enhance the oxidation resistance and mechanical toughness of free-standing film. The MXene@La–Ti–O film electrode shows excellent electrochemical performance with high capacitance of 663 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and high stability of 96% retention after 20,000 cycles. Moreover, the MXene@La–Ti–O symmetric supercapacitor exhibits superior energy storage performance with energy density of 58.93 Wh kg−1 at power density of 400 W kg−1, which is among the best performances reported so far for MXene-based flexible symmetric solid-state supercapacitors. The impressive results indicate the synergistic structural coupling strategy of MXene and La–Ti–O MOF is very promising for high-performance flexible supercapacitors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a free-standing Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene film with in-situ-grown La–Ti–O metal-organic framework, addressing MXene restacking, oxidation, and mechanical limitations. articles.excerpt_original: This dataset provides a density-functional-theory (DFT)-trained Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for atomistic simulations of twisted bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The potential employs the Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) representation and was developed to investigate structural reconstruction in moiré superlattices. Representative LAMMPS input files and an example bilayer hBN structure are also provided to facilitate the use of the potential. Simulations require a LAMMPS installation supporting the QUIP interface. The potential was developed for the study of stacking-dependent interlayer interactions and large-scale structural relaxation in twisted bilayer hBN, including the formation of AB/BA-like domains, domain-wall networks, and out-of-plane corrugation.
