articles.title_original: Two‐Dimensional Carrier Gas at Diamond and Cubic Boron Nitride (111) Interface: Role of Interfacial Bonding and Defects
articles.title_en: Diamond–Cubic Boron Nitride Interfaces Enable Tunable 2D Carrier Gases
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Diamond and cubic boron nitride (c‐BN) are promising ultrawide‐bandgap semiconductors for next‐generation high‐power and high‐frequency devices. Enabling these devices needs better understanding of interface electronic structure. Here, we investigate the effects of interfacial bonding and antisite point defects on the formation of two‐dimensional (2D) carrier gases at (111) diamond/c‐BN interfaces using hybrid density functional theory. c‐BN can be B‐ or N‐terminated. For each termination type, we identify two distinct interfacial bonding configurations, where a B (or N) atom is bonded to either one or three C atoms, resulting in four bonding types. Our results show that electron‐deficient C−B and electron‐rich C−N interfacial bonds result in 2D hole gas and 2D electron gas, respectively. Configurations with B (or N) bonded to three C atoms exhibit three times higher carrier density (1.3310 ) than those bonded to one C atom (4.4410 ). Furthermore, ‐type and ‐type antisite defects can stabilize C−B and C−N bonded interfaces, respectively, while reducing carrier density. Nevertheless, the carrier density remains high () even with these defects. This work may guide the engineering of diamond/c‐BN interfaces with tunable carrier densities for ‐ or ‐type conduction.
articles.summary_en: Hybrid density functional theory shows that interfacial bonding at diamond/cubic boron nitride (111) interfaces can produce either two-dimensional hole or electron gases. The findings indicate a route to engineering carrier density and conduction type in ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor devices, including effects from antisite defects.

articles.title_original: Water at the molecular frontier
articles.title_en: Molecular-Scale Water Challenges Bulk-Water Assumptions
articles.excerpt_original: Much of the water that matters most - flowing through biological cells and membranes, percolating through soils and rocks, or processed by filtration and desalination technologies - is not bulk water. It is water in nano- and molecular-scale confinement or at interfaces. Nanoscale water is therefore central to many challenges of our time, from the global water crisis and the water-energy nexus to catalysis, electrochemistry, and health. Beyond its applications, nanoscale water has emerged as a rich scientific field in its own right: discoveries are accumulating rapidly, revealing that confinement and interfacial forces produce a range of behaviours absent in the bulk. Sometimes this amounts to a renormalization of bulk properties; in other cases, new and non-intuitive phenomena emerge - exotic phases, anomalous transport, and dielectric responses that defy continuum expectations. A convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic devices, novel spectroscopies and microscopy approaches, and machine-learning-accelerated simulations is now exposing the molecular mechanisms behind these behaviours. This Perspective argues that the recent findings should not be viewed as isolated nanoscale anomalies, but as evidence for a molecular regime of water in which continuum descriptions must be rethought and molecular-level understanding becomes essential. Recognising and exploring this regime should have consequences ranging from fundamental physics to the rational design of future technologies that rely on water and dissolved ions.
articles.summary_en: A Perspective examines water confined at nanoscale interfaces and in molecular-scale environments, highlighting anomalous phases, transport, and dielectric behavior. It argues that molecular-level models could guide future filtration, desalination, catalysis, electrochemistry, and health technologies.

articles.title_original: 2D Organometallic Chalcogenide for Sub‐ppt Ratiometric Sensing
articles.title_en: PbBD Nanosensor Enables Sub-ppt NO₂ Detection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Semiconductor‐based sensors suffer from baseline drift that compromises measurement accuracy. Ratiometric sensing offers a solution by introducing a photoresponse internal reference, yet conventional materials face an inherent trade‐off between gas sensitivity and photoelectric stability. Here, we report a 2D organometallic chalcogenide, PbBD, featuring a multi‐quantum well structure composed of a continuous inorganic {PbS} n layer partially covered by compact and flexible organic ligands. This unique configuration exposes active sites on the inorganic layer, allowing gas molecules to directly interact with the inorganic semiconductor layer, bypassing the indirect electron transfer pathway typically imposed by functional groups. This direct interaction facilitates electron transfer efficiency and significantly enhances the sensitivity in gas sensing applications. The PbBD nanosheet‐based sensor achieves an ultrahigh response of 52900% to 10 ppm NO 2 and a ratiometric value of 0.84, which is 3.67 times higher than that of AgBDT. PbBD delivers both enhanced ratiometric sensitivity and an exceptionally low detection limit of 0.245 ppt, marking the lowest value ever reported for room‐temperature chemiresistive NO 2 sensing. Furthermore, the ratiometric mode reduces the coefficient of variation from 21.8% to 5.5% against temperature fluctuations. This work provides a strategy for co‐optimizing photoelectric and gas‐sensing properties toward high‐precision sensing applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a 2D organometallic chalcogenide nanosheet sensor with a 0.245-ppt room-temperature detection limit for NO₂. Its ratiometric mode also improves stability against temperature fluctuations, reducing the coefficient of variation from 21.8% to 5.5%.

articles.title_original: Sustainable laser-assisted processes for semiconductor manufacturing: a comprehensive review
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Sustainable Laser Processes for Semiconductor Manufacturing
articles.excerpt_original: Semiconductor manufacturing is essential for modern electronics, yet conventional fabrication relies heavily on high energy consumption and chemically intensive processes. As sustainability becomes imperative, alternative technologies that lower energy use and carbon footprints are urgently needed. This paper reviews the role of sustainable laser-based processes as potential green solutions for semiconductor manufacturing. We first outline the fundamental stages of conventional semiconductor fabrication alongside its primary sustainability challenges. Next, we summarize core laser-based processing mechanisms such as laser ablation, surface modification, and laser direct writing. The applications of these technologies across wafer processing, device fabrication, and advanced packaging are then evaluated, highlighting their potential for significant energy savings. Finally, a comparative sustainability assessment between laser-based and conventional methods is presented. Overall, laser-based manufacturing offers a versatile, energy-efficient, and low-footprint alternative, paving the way toward greener semiconductor production.
articles.summary_en: The review evaluates laser ablation, surface modification, and direct writing as lower-energy alternatives to conventional semiconductor fabrication. It covers applications in wafer processing, device fabrication, and advanced packaging, but reports no specific commercial deployment or company involvement.

articles.title_original: Magnetic excitons in a suspended 2D antiferromagnetic membrane
articles.title_en: Magnetic excitons observed in suspended NiPS₃ membranes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Layered magnetic and strongly correlated materials, such as NiPS 3 , present a rich platform for condensed matter physics with intrinsic properties intertwined by magnetism and low-dimensionality. A suspended light-emitting 2D antiferromagnetic membrane forms a highly controllable hybrid system in which the interplay between spin ordering, optical and mechanical degrees of freedom can be uniquely explored. NiPS 3 hosts excitons responsible for a puzzling luminescence down to a few atomic layers, linked to its zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The exact nature of these excitons remains unclear. Here we report on the magnetic excitons of a suspended few-layer NiPS 3 membrane. We reveal nematic zigzag states and study the optical transitions induced by the magnon-mediated motion of the excitation in the magnetic lattice, resulting in magnon-dressed excitons. We observe a strain tuning of these emission lines, dependent on their microscopic origin, with rates that indicate a strong localization of the magnetic excitons, fading with the number of magnon-mediated hops.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated magnon-dressed excitons in suspended few-layer nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS₃), revealing strain-tunable optical emission linked to antiferromagnetic order. The findings advance fundamental understanding of exciton–magnon interactions in low-dimensional materials, without an immediate commercial application.

articles.title_original: Stress induced semiconductor to semimetal transition and tunable optical anisotropy in puckered bilayer GeTe: a first-principles study
articles.title_en: Strain Tunes Bilayer GeTe from Semiconductor to Semimetal
articles.excerpt_original: In this study, Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to investigate a comparative analysis of structural, electronic, chemical bonding, phonon-dynamical, and optical properties of puckered monolayer and bilayer GeTe under applied tensile and compression stress ranging from − 1 to + 3 GPa. The indirect band gap is reduced by 76% compared to the monolayer (0.693 eV) in case of bilayer formation (0.166 eV). Under increasing biaxial compressive stress, the bilayer band gap progressively decreases and reaches a calculated zero-gap semimetallic state at approximately 0.55 GPa, characterized by band touching near the Γ point and the system is dynamically stable up to at least 3GPa, which was confirmed by phonon calculations. Based on Mulliken population analysis, the microscopic origin of gap closure is found to be progressive orbital rehybridization of Ge-Te bond. Compression is systematically red-shifted and amplified broadband optical absorption in direction dependent hierarchy inversion, leading to a mechanically tunable three-dimensional optical anisotropy. The results unveil puckered bilayer GeTe as a stress tunable platform for narrow-gap optoelectronics and pressure engineered quantum device architectures.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that puckered bilayer GeTe’s band gap narrows substantially under compression and reaches a zero-gap semimetallic state at about 0.55 GPa. The predicted stress-controlled optical anisotropy suggests potential applications in narrow-gap optoelectronics and pressure-engineered quantum devices.

articles.title_original: GaS–SnSSe heterostructure: A strain-tunable direct bandgap Rashba semiconductor
articles.title_en: Strain-Tunable GaS–SnSSe Rashba Semiconductor Demonstrated
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a GaS–SnSSe heterostructure with a strain-tunable direct bandgap and Rashba semiconductor behavior. The findings point to potential strain-engineered semiconductor and optoelectronic applications, although no device demonstration or commercial activity is reported.

articles.title_original: Unlocking Large-Area Two-Dimensional Transition Metal Dichalcogenides: From Epitaxial Growth to Frontier Applications
articles.title_en: Review Advances Wafer-Scale Growth of 2D Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Wafer-scale, high-quality, thickness- and stacking configuration-tunable two-dimensional (2D) semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides (STMDCs) hold great potential to serve as channel materials in complementary field effect transistors (CFETs) at the sub-nanometer technology node, thus further extending the logic technology roadmap. Epitaxial growth of 2D STMDCs on industrial-compatible substrates should be the first step. In this perspective, we present an overview of recent advances in the epitaxial mechanism explorations and wafer-scale growth of monolayer STMDC films or single crystals via substrate surface modulations and growth methodology optimizations. The applications of 2D STMDC wafers in high-performance electronic and optoelectronic devices are reviewed. Challenges and prospects are also highlighted, especially regarding the 12-inch-scale preparations of monolayer STMDC films and functional device integration.
articles.summary_en: The perspective reviews epitaxial growth of wafer-scale, tunable 2D transition-metal dichalcogenide films and single crystals on industrial-compatible substrates. It assesses applications in advanced transistors and optoelectronic devices, while highlighting challenges in 12-inch monolayer production and integration.

articles.title_original: Processing-Tuned Laser-Induced Graphene Transducers for Polyaniline pH Sensors
articles.title_en: Laser-Processing Optimization Improves Graphene-Based Polyaniline pH Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Flexible pH sensors are important for wearable, biomedical, environmental, and process-monitoring applications, but achieving simple, scalable fabrication while maintaining high sensing performance remains challenging. Laser-induced graphene (LIG) has emerged as a promising transducer material because it enables direct laser patterning of porous, conductive graphitized carbon electrodes on flexible substrates. Although laser-processing conditions are known to affect LIG morphology, graphitization, and electrical properties, their influence on pH-sensitive layer formation and pH-sensing performance has not been systematically investigated. In this study, polyaniline (PANi)-modified LIG pH sensors were fabricated using four laser-processing combinations of laser power and scan speed. The resulting LIG and PANi/LIG electrodes were characterized using sheet-resistance measurements, optical microscopy, SEM, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS. PANi was electropolymerized on the LIG working electrodes under identical cyclic voltammetry conditions, and the assembled sensors were evaluated in pH 4–9 buffer solutions. The results showed that laser processing produced distinct LIG morphologies, porosities, sheet resistance, and PANi coverage, leading to different sensing performances. Among the samples, PANi/LIG-9.2–350, fabricated at 9.2 W and 350 mm/s, exhibited the best overall performance, with a near-Nernstian sensitivity of −60.04 mV/pH, a 12 h drift rate of 1.67 mV/h, hysteresis of 2.06 mV, and rapid response time of 13.2 s. These findings emphasize the significance of laser-processing-dependent LIG microstructure and electrical properties in governing PANi deposition behavior and resulting potentiometric pH-sensing performance.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers showed that laser power and scan speed significantly affect laser-induced graphene morphology, polyaniline coverage, and pH-sensing performance. The best device achieved near-Nernstian sensitivity of −60.04 mV/pH, a 13.2-second response time, and low drift across pH 4–9.

articles.title_original: Green Manufacturing of High-Performance Multilayered Boron Nitride Composites via Modulus-Contrast-Assisted Stack Pressing
articles.title_en: Modulus-Contrast Pressing Produces Large-Area, Thermally Anisotropic Boron Nitride Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Controlling the in-plane orientation of two-dimensional nanosheets during repeated forming remains challenging because deformation can become nonuniform through the film thickness. Here, alternating 60 and 80 wt % boron nitride nanosheet/thermoplastic polyurethane (BNNS/TPU) layers were used to introduce a moderate modulus contrast during water-based stack pressing and were compared with homogeneous 70 wt % films having the same nominal average filler content. Repeated pressing increased BNNS alignment in both architectures, while the binary film exhibited a slightly narrower SEM-derived angular distribution after six total pressing operations. The binary film reached an in-plane thermal conductivity of 17.85 W m–1·K–1, a through-plane thermal conductivity of 0.22 W m–1 K–1, a tensile strength of 17.48 MPa, and a thermal anisotropy ratio of approximately 81. Under the present point-heating configuration, its hotspot temperature was 5.7 °C lower than that of the unitary film at 60 s. Idealized linear-elastic finite-element analysis qualitatively illustrates modulus-dependent stress and strain partitioning but does not model interfacial damage or nanosheet rotation. Fabrication of 400 × 400 mm films further demonstrates large-area batch-processing feasibility.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed multilayer boron nitride nanosheet/thermoplastic polyurethane films using water-based stack pressing, achieving 17.85 W m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in-plane thermal conductivity and a thermal anisotropy ratio of about 81. Fabrication of 400 × 400 mm films indicates potential for scalable thermal-management materials.

articles.title_original: Two‐Dimensional Magnetic Materials From Ferromagnetism to Altermagnetism: Fabrication, Symmetry, Evidence, and Device Readiness
articles.title_en: Review Maps 2D Magnetic Materials from Ferromagnetism to Altermagnetism
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Atomically thin magnets are governed by composition, thickness, stacking, strain, defects, substrates, ferroic order, and interfaces. This Review organizes two‐dimensional (2D) magnetism using net magnetization and momentum‐space spin splitting or spin‐polarization patterns as primary coordinates, supplemented by sublattice structure and the symmetry relations between opposite‐spin sublattices. Ferromagnets generally carry a net moment; ferrimagnets can be fully compensated. Conventional antiferromagnets may retain spin‐degenerate bands, while altermagnets permit nonrelativistic alternating spin splitting under dimension‐specific symmetry constraints. M1–M4 reporting classes introduced here distinguish layer‐resolved atomically thin forms, non‐layer‐resolved thin flakes or films, bulk benchmarks, and theoretical candidates or design routes; the evidence category and ordering‐temperature provenance are reported independently. Current experimental support for altermagnetism comes mainly from M2 thin‐film and M3 bulk benchmarks, leaving a fully verified atomically thin M1 altermagnetic phase as an open experimental goal. Most proposed monolayer and few‐layer systems therefore fall within M4, and contested cases clarify the measurements needed for phase assignment. Device readiness is compared qualitatively using operating temperature, readout, switching, domain control, stability, scalability, interface sensitivity, and integration difficulty. Reliable phase assignment and device assessment require complementary measurements from the same material form under matched conditions, ideally on the same specimen or in situ.
articles.summary_en: A Wiley review organizes atomically thin magnetic materials by magnetization, spin splitting, symmetry, and evidence quality. It finds that experimentally supported altermagnetism remains concentrated in thin films and bulk benchmarks, while fully verified atomically thin phases and practical device integration remain open challenges.

articles.title_original: Mo2CTx-MXene/NiO hybrid nanostructure for selective non-enzymatic glucose detection
articles.title_en: Mo₂CTx MXene/NiO Hybrid Enables Selective Non-Enzymatic Glucose Detection
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a Mo₂CTx MXene/NiO hybrid nanostructure for selective, non-enzymatic glucose detection. The work signals a potential materials platform for electrochemical glucose sensors, although no performance or commercialization details are provided.

articles.title_original: Tribological performance and tribofilm formation of hBN-enhanced glycerol-based lubricants
articles.title_en: hBN-Enhanced Glycerol Lubricants Reduce Friction and Form Protective Tribofilms
articles.excerpt_original: The development of sustainable lubricants that effectively reduce friction and wear remains challenging, particularly under boundary and mixed lubrication conditions. Incorporating solid lubricant additives is a promising approach to improve the tribological performance of biodegradable lubricants. Among these additives, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has attracted considerable attention because of its layered structure and low shear strength. Nevertheless, its tribological behaviour and tribochemical interactions in glycerol-based lubricants remain insufficiently understood. In this work, pure glycerol and aqueous glycerol containing 0.02 and 0.1 wt% hBN were evaluated in steel/steel contacts using a reciprocating ball-on-disc tribometer under normal loads of 3 and 40 N. Among the investigated formulations, 0.1 wt% hBN provided the best tribological performance. Under a load of 40 N, the addition of 0.1 wt% hBN reduced the steady-state coefficient of friction from ~0.10 to ~0.05 in pure glycerol and from ~0.09 to ~0.04 in aqueous glycerol. The effect on wear morphology depended on the base fluid, with the maximum penetration depth decreasing in the glycerol system but increasing in the aqueous glycerol system, despite a reduction in wear-track width. FTIR, Raman, and XPS analyses revealed tribochemical interactions and the formation of a protective hybrid tribofilm. The hBN-derived material present within the tribofilm underwent less pronounced structural modification in pure glycerol than in aqueous glycerol. These findings demonstrate the potential of hBN-modified glycerol lubricants for environmentally friendly boundary and mixed lubrication applications.
articles.summary_en: Academic research finds that 0.1 wt% hexagonal boron nitride reduced friction by roughly half in glycerol-based steel contacts under high load. The additive formed a protective tribofilm, supporting potential use in biodegradable boundary and mixed lubrication systems, although wear effects varied with the fluid composition.

articles.title_original: Optoelectrical Conditioning in Graphene Quantum Dot‍–‍Vanadium Oxide Artificial Synapse
articles.title_en: Graphene Quantum Dot–Vanadium Oxide Synapse Enables Optoelectronic Learning
articles.excerpt_original: Neuromorphic computing requires artificial synaptic devices capable of adaptive learning and memory retention. Here, we present a monolithically integrated optoelectronic synaptic device based on a 0D/3D Ag/graphene quantum dot–vanadium oxide (GQD–VO 2 )/Ni heterojunction exhibiting stimulation‐history‐dependent conductance modulation. The device supports synaptic modulation under electrical, optical, and combined optoelectrical stimulation, with enhanced optoelectronic response compared with the bare VO 2 device. Repeated optoelectrical stimulation modifies the retained device state and subsequent potentiation–depression characteristics, a process described here as optoelectrical conditioning. This evolution is evaluated using retained current ( I ), fitted potentiation–depression time constants ( τ ), and nonlinearity coefficients. Wavelength‐dependent optical associative learning with positive and negative reinforcement is further demonstrated under different optical stimuli. Performance evaluation using Fashion‐MNIST and Digit‐MNIST datasets show improved classification accuracy with the progression of optoelectrical conditioning learning cycles, increasing from 81.53% to 84.13% and from 91.71% to 95.58%, respectively. Monte Carlo simulations further indicate improved classification accuracy across multiple runs following repeated learning cycles. Furthermore, this behavior is illustrated through reconstructed Fashion‐MNIST image outputs with the repeated learning cycles. These findings highlight the potential of Ag/GQD–VO 2 /Ni device for neuromorphic applications, advancing AI‐integrated bio‐inspired computing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a monolithically integrated Ag/graphene quantum dot–VO₂/Ni artificial synapse supporting electrical, optical, and combined optoelectrical stimulation. Repeated conditioning improved simulated Fashion-MNIST and Digit-MNIST classification accuracy, indicating potential for neuromorphic semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: Oriented Spiral Growth of Two-Dimensional Materials
articles.title_en: Oriented Spiral WS₂ Films Enable Scalable Twistronics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) spiral growth is crucial for scalable moiré superlattices, yet controlled large-area synthesis remains an outstanding challenge. Here, we report a rational epitaxial strategy for synthesizing oriented spiral WS2 films on a-plane sapphire, where unidirectionally aligned R-stacked domains serve as templates and substrate tilting acts as the key trigger for spiral growth. Comprehensive characterization confirms high density, identical crystallographic orientation, zero interlayer twist, well-defined R-stacking, and excellent crystalline quality across these structures. We propose a two-stage growth model: dual-coupling-guided formation of aligned R-stacked domains transitions into a dual-mode process for simultaneous lateral coalescence and vertical screw-dislocation-driven growth. The unique configuration of these oriented-spiral films endows photodetectors with superior performance and an extended spectral response. Our work represents a significant advance in 2D spiral materials, establishing a key step toward robust and scalable twistronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an epitaxial strategy for producing large-area, crystallographically aligned spiral WS₂ films on tilted a-plane sapphire. The structures show strong photodetector performance and extended spectral response, supporting scalable two-dimensional materials synthesis for twistronics and optoelectronics.

articles.title_en: Lewis-Acid Engineering Modulates MXene-Supported Ir/Ru Clusters for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution

articles.title_original: Intersection of many-body physics and photonics: 2D semiconductors and photonic integrated circuits
articles.title_en: Dissertation Demonstrates Tunable TMD Nanocavities for Photonic Devices
articles.excerpt_original: This dissertation explores the intersection of many-body physics and photonics. While the toolbox of photonics provides powerful means to probe, manipulate, and even simulate matter, insights from many-body physics can, in turn, guide the design of devices with desirable optical properties. In this pursuit, we use two complementary material platforms: (i) atomically-thin transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) semiconductors, where strong excitonic interactions and moir\'e superlattices enable emergent many-body phenomena; and (ii) CMOS-compatible silicon nitride photonic integrated circuits, where topology and nonlinearity give rise to a new regime of exploring topological photonic devices for practical applications. First, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a sub-wavelength two-dimensional nanocavity using two atomically thin TMD mirrors with degenerate resonances. Angle-resolved measurements show a flat band, which sets this system apart from conventional photonic cavities. We demonstrate how the excitonic nature of the mirrors enables the formation of chiral and tunable optical modes upon the application of an external magnetic field. Moreover, we show the electrical tunability of the confined mode. Our work demonstrates a mechanism for confining light with high-quality excitonic materials, opening avenues for spin-photon interfaces and chiral cavity electrodynamics. Second, we explore the interplay between fermionic and bosonic populations in a lattice, using a TMD heterobilayer device that hosts this hybrid particle density. We independently tune the fermionic and bosonic populations by electronic doping and optical injection of electron-hole pairs, respectively. articles.summary_en: Research demonstrates sub-wavelength nanocavities using atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenide mirrors, with chiral, electrically tunable optical modes. The work also investigates interacting excitons in TMD heterobilayers and topological photonic devices on silicon nitride circuits.

articles.title_original: Shear Assisted Diamond Formation in Cold-Compressed HOPG
articles.title_en: Shear Enables Diamond Formation from Graphite at Lower Pressure
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Diamond synthesis from a graphite precursor is primarily constrained by the requirement for the simultaneous application of extreme pressures and temperatures. We explore the microstructural changes in highly oriented pyrolytic graphite subject to shear during room temperature compression. Using a diamond anvil cell, nonhydrostatic pressures of up to 160 GPa were applied, resulting in an optically transparent, diamond-like material above 80 GPa that reverted to an opaque, largely graphite-like material upon decompression. Detailed microstructural analysis of the recovered sample revealed nanoscale diamond-like domains embedded within a graphitic matrix containing shear bands and localized basal slip features consistent with a high shear environment. Employing a rotational diamond anvil cell greatly enhanced these shear-induced features, producing significant amounts of diamond in samples recovered from applied pressures as low as 15 GPa. These findings demonstrate that shear can facilitate the graphite-to-diamond transformation, enabling sp3 bond formation under conditions where extreme temperatures are not required.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that shear during room-temperature compression can drive graphite-to-diamond transformation without extreme temperatures. Rotational compression produced substantial diamond at pressures as low as 15 GPa, suggesting a potentially lower-energy synthesis route.

articles.title_original: Computational screening of reconfigurable van der Waals ferroelectric semiconductor heterojunctions for all-in-one optoelectronic devices
articles.title_en: Computationally designed ferroelectric heterojunctions enable reconfigurable optoelectronics
articles.excerpt_original: Reconfigurable optoelectronic devices based on two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals semiconductor heterojunctions (VSHs) are potential candidates for multifunctional applications in a single device. However, device multifunctionalities highly rely on VSHs with tunable band alignment and band offsets for achieving reconfigurable optoelectronic properties. Herein, we report a new class of 2D VSHs consisting of atomically thin ABP2X6-type ferroelectric (FE) semiconductors for the development of an all-in-one optoelectronic architecture based on high-throughput first-principles calculations and the nonequilibrium Green’s function method. Our results reveal that the polarization coupling of dual FE layers in the VSHs leads to multiple polarization states, allowing a sequential band-alignment evolution. Using CuInP2S6/AuInP2S6 VSHs as a prototype example, we demonstrate the heterojunction with reversible band-alignment transitions and tunable band offsets by modulating the polarization state of dual FE layers. This enables the device to achieve a theoretical tunneling electroresistance ratio (TER) of 106% between the interlayer FE and antiferroelectric (AFE) states at the bias voltage of 1.5 V, as well as positive and negative photoresponses. The FE-polarization-dependent band alignment and photoresponse of the heterojunction device can be used to implement in-sensor broadband convolutional processing for image recognition and reconfigurable optoelectronic logic operations including AND, OR, and XOR. These findings suggest huge potential of 2D FE VSHs for exploiting multifunctional optoelectronic device applications.
articles.summary_en: First-principles and nonequilibrium Green’s-function calculations identify 2D ferroelectric semiconductor heterojunctions with polarization-controlled band alignment and tunable photoresponses. A CuInP2S6/AuInP2S6 prototype is predicted to support tunneling electroresistance, broadband in-sensor processing, and reconfigurable AND, OR, and XOR logic.

articles.title_en: MXene–Porous Carbon Electrodes for High-Performance Supercapacitors

articles.title_original: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene
articles.title_en: First-principles study identifies irida-graphane as a stable wide-band-gap semiconductor
articles.excerpt_original: Opening a band gap in metallic two-dimensional carbon allotropes is an important step toward their use in electronic and optoelectronic devices, and full hydrogenation has proven to be an effective route to achieve it. Here, we propose irida-graphane, the fully hydrogenated derivative of the irida-graphene, a monolayer composed of three-, six-, and eight-membered rings, and investigate its structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory (DFT) at the PBE and HSE06 levels combined with phonon and \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. All carbon atoms adopt $sp^3$ hybridization, with the hydrogen atoms of the three- and six-membered rings bonded to opposite sides of a buckled carbon framework, and the lattice parameter contracts by 4.3% with respect to irida-graphene. The hydrogenation energy of $-0.53$ eV/H indicates that the hydrogenation of irida-graphene from molecular hydrogen is exothermic. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies confirms the dynamical stability of irida-graphane, and AIMD simulations show that its structure remains intact at temperatures up to 2000 K. Irida-graphane is mechanically isotropic, with an in-plane stiffness of approximately 156 N/m, a Poisson's ratio of approximately 0.1, and critical strains of approximately 20%. Hydrogenation transforms the metallic parent structure into a semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 4.68 eV (PBE) and 6.0 eV (HSE06). Irida-graphane is transparent in the visible range, with reflectivity below 0.3%, and absorbs strongly in the deep ultraviolet, with absorption coefficients of the order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ cm$^{-1}$. These results suggest irida-graphane as a candidate wide-gap material for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coating
articles.summary_en: Density-functional theory and molecular-dynamics simulations suggest that fully hydrogenated irida-graphene is dynamically stable up to 2,000 K and has an indirect band gap of up to 6.0 eV. The predicted transparency and strong deep-UV absorption indicate potential for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings, but the findings remain theoretical.

articles.title_original: Colloquium: A critique on van der Waals and two-dimensional magnets
articles.title_en: APS Colloquium Critiques van der Waals and Two-Dimensional Magnets
articles.summary_en: This academic colloquium examines and critiques prevailing concepts surrounding van der Waals materials and two-dimensional magnets. It is relevant to ongoing research assessment in low-dimensional magnetism, but no specific applications or commercial outcomes are identified.

articles.title_original: Graphene Polymer Composite Electrodes, for Triboelectric Energy Harvesting
articles.title_en: Graphene–polymer electrodes improve triboelectric energy harvesting
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Sustainable distributed energy technologies are increasingly in demand to power the growing ecosystem of low-power electronics and sensors without frequent battery replacement, and triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have emerged as a promising route for harvesting abundant mechanical energy. However, challenges persist in scalable, low-cost and eco-friendly electrode fabrication with balanced electrical performance, film integrity, and triboelectric efficiency. This study develops graphene-polymer composite electrodes via liquid-phase shear-force exfoliation of expanded graphite in isopropanol (IPA)/water mixtures, followed by vacuum filtration onto polyethylene (PE) films. Multilayer graphene (MLG) suspensions were optimized at shear speeds of 5000−7000 rpm for 1 h and volumes of 10−40 mL, with 7000 rpm and 40 mL yielding the best electrical performance due to reduced flake size and improved film continuity. Different additives were incorporated directly during film formation to enhance properties such as electrical conductivity and film integrity. The inclusion of 1% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) improved adhesion and flexibility, albeit at the expense of electrical conductivity, while 1.3% poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) enhanced film continuity and exhibited the lowest sheet resistance but introduced brittleness and agglomeration. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed multilayer graphene–polymer composite electrodes on polyethylene films using liquid-phase exfoliation and vacuum filtration. Pristine graphene electrodes delivered about 90 V, 1.1 μA and 32 nC, while PEDOT:PSS additives produced a maximum power density of 0.45 W m−2 despite reduced flexibility and increased brittleness.

articles.title_original: Direct imaging elucidates ionic memory in two-dimensional nanochannels
articles.title_en: Direct imaging reveals the mechanism behind ionic memory in 2D nanochannels
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nanofluidic memristors promise brain-inspired information processing with ions, yet their microscopic origin remains debated. So far, ionic memory has been attributed to ion-specific interactions, dynamic wetting, chemical reactions or mechanical deformations, yet typically without direct experimental evidence. Here, by combining operando interferometric imaging with electrokinetic measurements, we directly visualize voltage-induced blistering of the confining walls of two-dimensional (2D) nanochannels as the key origin of memristive hysteresis. We identify two distinct classes of blisters: unidirectional, driven by electrostatic forces on surface charges, and bidirectional, arising from osmotic pressure due to concentration polarization. This mechanistic framework explains device evolution and device-to-device variability, and reframes stochastic blistering as a functional design element. Our results constitute a direct proof of electromechanical coupling as a robust pathway to ionic memory in 2D nanochannels and open routes towards high-performance ionic memristors and electrically actuated nanofluidic valves.

articles.title_original: Two-dimensional quantum droplets and vortices in Rydberg-dressed Bose gases
articles.title_en: Rydberg-Dressed Bose Gases Host Stable 2D Quantum Droplets and Vortices
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We systematically explore isotropic self-bound liquid states and topological vortex excitations in two-dimensional binary Bose-Einstein condensates with tunable Rydberg soft-core interactions, modeled by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation incorporating the two-dimensional Lee-Huang-Yang quantum correction. Combining analytical Thomas-Fermi treatment with high-precision numerical simulations, we obtain stable fundamental and vortex-carrying quantum droplet solutions and investigate their collisional dynamics. The particle number N and Rydberg coupling strength κ are shown to systematically modulate the spatial and thermodynamic properties of both vortex-free and ring-shaped vortex liquids. In the repulsive regime κ > 0, our results agree quantitatively with those of magnetic quadrupolar condensates, confirming a common stabilization scenario for two-dimensional quantum fluids. More importantly, the Rydberg system distinguishes itself by offering fully isotropic, sign-switchable interactions and sustaining stable vortex droplets with winding numbers up to m = 4 over broad parameter ranges—features that are severely constrained in anisotropic quadrupolar counterparts.Collisions between moving zero-vorticity and vortex self-bound droplets are briefly discussed, demonstrate that their collisional dynamics are universal under the competing nonlocal repulsion and the logarithmic Lee-Huang-Yang effect.
articles.summary_en: Researchers model two-dimensional binary Bose–Einstein condensates with tunable Rydberg interactions and identify stable self-bound droplets, including vortices with winding numbers up to four. The system offers isotropic, sign-switchable interactions and universal collision dynamics distinct from anisotropic magnetic quadrupolar condensates.

articles.title_original: Functional MXene Inks for Printed Electronics: Chemistry, Rheology, and Devices
articles.title_en: MXene Inks Advance Printed Electronics and Flexible Devices
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXene‐based functional inks have emerged as a promising platform for printed electronics by combining high electrical conductivity, tunable surface chemistry, and solution processability. This review establishes a unified framework linking MXene synthesis, surface engineering, ink rheology, printing behavior, and device performance across diverse additive manufacturing technologies. Particular emphasis is placed on how chemical functionalization, composite design, and interfacial engineering influence colloidal stability, printability, and functionality. By elucidating structure–ink–process–property relationships, the review reveals how MXene chemistry and rheology govern printed microstructure and performance in sensors, energy‐storage devices, and electromagnetic interference shielding systems. Despite rapid progress, widespread implementation remains constrained by three interconnected challenges: ensuring long‐term chemical and colloidal stability, achieving printability without sacrificing electrical transport, and establishing scalable, reproducible manufacturing routes. Future advances will depend on oxidation‐resistant formulations, manufacturing‐aware rheological design, sustainable processing strategies, and standardized evaluation protocols. These developments provide a roadmap for translating MXene inks from laboratory‐scale demonstrations to reliable, high‐performance flexible and multifunctional electronic systems.
articles.summary_en: This review links MXene chemistry, rheology, printing behavior, and device performance across additive manufacturing methods. It identifies stability, printability, scalable manufacturing, and standardized evaluation as key barriers to commercialization in sensors, energy storage, and electromagnetic-interference shielding.

articles.title_original: MXene-bioinspired nanomaterials for biosensing of pharmaceuticals and personal care products in complex aquatic systems at ultra-trace levels
articles.title_en: MXene Nanomaterials Advance Ultra-Trace Aquatic Pollutant Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) are an increasing class of environmental pollutants of concern in aquatic ecosystems owing to their persistence and biological activity at low concentrations. Correct and selective monitoring of these substances is necessary to assess their ecological impacts and preserve water quality. The high conductivity, large surface area and tunable surface chemistry of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) have recently opened new avenues for electrochemical sensing. In this study we explain the state of the art of MXene nanoparticles, their characteristics, production and functionalization procedures that allow the integration of these materials in electrochemical and bioinspired sensing systems. Design advances such as biomimetic recognition elements, molecular imprinting, enzymes and nanocomposites are critically reviewed in terms of their contribution towards improving selectivity and operational stability of sensors. This study examines the analytical performance of MXene-based sensors for the ultra-trace detection of PPCPs in complex aquatic matrices, focusing on advances in sensitivity, antifouling strategies, and multiplexed detection. It also discusses future perspectives such as smart sensor networks and AI-driven data analytics, as well as issues in material scalability, sensor durability and real-world deployment. This study opens the door for the new potential of MXene-enabled platforms for the development of environmental analytical chemistry and shows the future research pathways towards sustainable and effective aquatic pollution monitoring.
articles.summary_en: The review examines MXene-based electrochemical and bioinspired sensors for detecting pharmaceuticals and personal care products in complex aquatic environments. It highlights biomimetic recognition, molecular imprinting, antifouling strategies and multiplexed detection, while identifying scalability, durability and deployment as remaining challenges.

articles.title_original: MXene-Integrated Ni–Hf Nanoflowers for Efficient Water Splitting in Alkaline Wastewater: Experimental and DFT Insights
articles.title_en: MXene–Ni–Hf Nanoflowers Enable Wastewater Electrolysis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) is a promising technology for producing green hydrogen. Unfortunately, the requirements for purified water, costs, and current limitations restrict its application. We proposed solutions to these barriers by employing wastewater effluents and an efficient MXene-based model electrocatalyst (NiHf-LDH/MXene/NF). In a two-electrode cell configuration, it requires 1.89, 1.92, 1.95, and 1.98 V for deionized water (DI), tertiary effluent (TE), secondary effluent (SE) from an external membrane bioreactor (eMBR), and the activated sludge process (ASP) to attain 1000 mA/cm2, outperforming benchmark electrocatalysts (Pt/C∥IrO2). Durability was evaluated at 650 mA/cm2 for 200 h in wastewater effluent, with a 0.603 mV/h drop. The system’s energy efficiency was 71.7 and 60.5% (based on the lower heating value (LHV)) at 100 and 1000 mA/cm2, respectively. Moreover, pollutant levels decreased: chemical oxygen demand (COD) (47.2%), total nitrogen (TN) (49.7%), turbidity (53.8%), and total dissolved solids (TDS) (5.7%). Density functional theory (DFT) indicates that the model electrocatalyst features an excellent adsorption energy (0.51 eV) for water molecules, which favors electrochemical reactions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an MXene-based Ni–Hf layered double hydroxide electrocatalyst for alkaline water splitting using wastewater effluents. The system reached up to 1,000 mA/cm², operated for 200 hours, and simultaneously reduced several wastewater pollutants.

articles.title_original: A magnesium-engineered nanoporous MXene/GelMA hydrogel platform for photothermal eradication of bacteria and accelerated bone healing
articles.title_en: Magnesium-Engineered MXene Hydrogel Supports Bone Repair and Photothermal Antibacterial Activity
articles.excerpt_original: Bone defect repair remains clinically challenging because of insufficient osteogenic regeneration and the potential risk of postoperative infection. Developing multifunctional biomaterials that integrate osteogenic regulation with antibacterial potential is highly desirable. In this study, a magnesium-engineered nanoporous MXene/GelMA hydrogel, termed nMX/Gel, was constructed by incorporating microwave-assisted combustion engineered nMX into a GelMA hydrogel matrix. Compared with conventional MXene/GelMA hydrogel (MX/Gel), nMX/Gel exhibited enhanced photothermal performance under 1064 nm near-infrared irradiation. In vitro antibacterial assays showed that nMX effectively inhibited the growth of Escherichia coli and S. aureus upon near-infrared irradiation, confirming its photothermal antibacterial potential. Furthermore, nMX/Gel showed favorable cytocompatibility and promoted MC3T3-E1 cell proliferation. In addition, nMX/Gel significantly upregulated the expression of osteogenesis-related genes, including ALP, RUNX2, and OPN, in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. In a rat femoral defect model, micro-CT, histological staining, and immunohistochemical analyses further confirmed that nMX/Gel markedly enhanced new bone formation, collagen deposition, and the expression of osteogenic markers OCN and OPN. Overall, this designed nMX/Gel hydrogel provides a promising multifunctional biomaterial strategy for bone defect repair by combining enhanced osteogenic activity with photothermal antibacterial potential.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a magnesium-engineered nanoporous MXene/GelMA hydrogel that combines near-infrared photothermal antibacterial activity with osteogenic effects. In rat femoral-defect models, the hydrogel enhanced new bone formation and collagen deposition, indicating potential for multifunctional bone repair.

articles.title_original: Controlled oxidative polymerization of thiophene on oxidation-sensitive Ti3C2Tx MXene for enhanced supercapacitor performance
articles.title_en: Controlled Polythiophene Growth Improves MXene Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: Integrating conducting polymers with Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene offers an attractive strategy for enhancing supercapacitor performance, yet direct oxidative polymerization remains challenging because the oxidants required for polymer formation simultaneously promote rapid MXene degradation. Herein, we demonstrate that successful aqueous in-situ polymerization depends on controlling the kinetic competition between polythiophene growth and oxidative degradation of MXene. Prolonged exposure to ammonium persulfate resulted in extensive oxidation of Ti 3 C 2 T x into anatase TiO 2 , whereas limiting the reaction time to ≤1.5 h preserved the layered MXene framework while enabling conformal polythiophene growth. Structural and spectroscopic characterization by XRD, TEM, FTIR, UV–Vis, Raman, and XPS confirmed preservation of the MXene architecture, successful polythiophene growth, and the formation of an electronically coupled MXene–polythiophene interface. Electrochemical measurements further revealed that the optimized nanocomposite balanced electric double-layer and pseudocapacitive charge storage while delivering the highest specific capacitance and best cycling stability among all investigated materials, outperforming both pristine MXene and polythiophene. A symmetric supercapacitor assembled from the nanocomposite delivered a specific capacitance of 30.48 F/g at 1 mV/s and 27.63 F/g at 5 A/g, retained 84.2% of its initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles, and achieved an energy density of 0.61 Wh/kg at a power density of 1000 W/kg. articles.summary_en: Researchers controlled oxidative polymerization of polythiophene on Ti3C2Tx MXene to limit oxidation while forming an electronically coupled nanocomposite. The optimized material achieved 84.2% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles, with 0.61 Wh/kg energy density at 1,000 W/kg.

articles.title_original: Theoretical study of high-order harmonic generation in solids based on deep-learning methods
articles.title_en: Deep-learning method models temperature-dependent high-harmonic generation in solids
articles.excerpt_original: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids provides a compact and coherent EUV radiation, which has attracted considerable attention. Many theoretical methods for laser-crystal interactions are developed. However, an approach to treat large-scale amorphous systems with ab-initio accuracy is still lacking because of the enormous computational cost. Here, we incorporate molecular dynamics and tight-binding electron Hamiltonians based on deep-learning methods to solve the problem efficiently. Its accuracy is validated by comparing the HHG spectra of monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) with those obtained using existing methods. Then we use it to study the temperature-dependent HHG in bulk Si. We uncover a distinct harmonic-order-dependent thermal response: low-order harmonics are enhanced with increasing temperature, whereas high-order harmonics are suppressed. The former is caused by the modification of the inter-site hopping in the system, while the latter is mainly influenced by the structural disorder induced by the thermal effects, in agreement with experimental observations. This work establishes a scalable computational strategy for investigating HHG in solids and provides new insights into the interplay between lattice fluctuations and ultrafast electron dynamics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable computational approach combining molecular dynamics, tight-binding Hamiltonians and deep learning to model high-harmonic generation in large amorphous systems. The study validates the method using monolayer hexagonal boron nitride and finds that temperature enhances low-order harmonics but suppresses high-order harmonics in bulk silicon.

articles.title_original: Interlayer-Engineered Schottky Barrier and Rectification at Metal/ β -Ga 2 O 3 Interfaces from First Principles
articles.title_en: 2D Interlayers Tune Schottky Rectification in β-Ga₂O₃ Contacts
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Using DFT-NEGF simulations with the TB-mBJ exchange potential, we investigate Schottky barrier formation and carrier transport in metal/β-Ga 2 O 3 (100) contacts. For Ni, Ti, Ag, and Au contacts at a donor concentration of 1 × 10 19 cm -3 , Au exhibits pronounced forward rectification, while Ag, Ti, and Ni display degraded or reversed rectification due to metal-induced gap states (MIGS) that enhance Fermi-level pinning and tunneling. Inserting a monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) interlayer into the Ag contact suppresses MIGS, shifting the dominant transport mechanism from quantum tunneling to thermionic emission and restoring forward rectification. In contrast, a polar Janus WSSe interlayer creates an interfacial built-in electric field that yields reverse rectification relative to the h-BN-interlayered contact. However, the Janus-interlayered contact exhibits a small current. Reversing the WSSe orientation to WSeS changes the transport response, but the effect is not a simple mirror image. These results provide design rules for choosing metals, doping levels, and 2D interlayers to suppress MIGS and tailor Schottky rectification in ultra-wide-bandgap β -Ga 2 O 3 electronics.
articles.summary_en: First-principles simulations show that metal choice and 2D interlayers strongly affect Schottky barriers and rectification in β-Ga₂O₃ electronics. An h-BN monolayer suppresses metal-induced gap states and restores forward rectification, while Janus WSSe enables low-current reverse rectification.

articles.title_original: A van der Waals Floating-Gate Platform for Broadband Optoelectronic Neuromorphic Computing
articles.title_en: Van der Waals Floating-Gate Device Enables Broadband Neuromorphic Computing
articles.excerpt_original: Artificial synapses that integrate nonvolatile memory with broadband optoelectronic learning are essential for next-generation neuromorphic computing. However, their realization remains challenging because conventional floating-gate memories exhibit limited optical functionality and poor scalability. Here, we report a van der Waals ReS2/hBN/InSe floating-gate synaptic transistor that combines efficient charge storage with broadband optoelectronic learning in a single device architecture. The heterostructure incorporates InSe as a floating-gate layer for stable charge storage, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) as a tunneling dielectric, and ReS2 as a photoresponsive channel, enabling carrier tunneling under electrical and optical stimulation. Through the combined operation of these layers, the device achieves a large memory window, an on/off current ratio exceeding 10^6, stable multilevel conductance states, and reliable retention over 10^4 s. Broadband visible-to-near-infrared optical excitation enables controllable synaptic weight modulation and the emulation of essential synaptic functions, including short- and long-term plasticity, paired-pulse facilitation, and pulse-amplitude- and pulse-duration-dependent plasticity. Optical potentiation and electrical depression further enable bidirectional modulation of synaptic weights. Beyond these synaptic functions, the device demonstrates higher-order learning through associative and discrimination conditioning inspired by the Pavlovian learning paradigm, as well as reconfigurable Boolean logic driven by electro-optical inputs. These results establish a multifunctional van der Waals floating-gate platform that integrates nonvolatile memory, broadband optoelectronic learning, and adaptive information processing within a single tr
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a ReS2/hBN/InSe floating-gate synaptic transistor combining nonvolatile memory with broadband visible-to-near-infrared optoelectronic learning. The device demonstrates multilevel conductance, long retention, synaptic plasticity, associative learning, and reconfigurable Boolean logic.

articles.title_original: UVA-VUV broadband photodetector based on a p-hBN/n-ZnO heterojunction
articles.title_en: hBN–ZnO heterojunction enables high-performance UVA–VUV photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: Ultraviolet photodetectors have been extensively investigated, whereas achieving high-performance photodetection in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) spectral region remains relatively challenging. In this work, a p-hBN/n-ZnO heterojunction UVA-VUV broadband ultraviolet photodetector was fabricated with wavelength-dependent trap-assisted gain modulation. The device exhibits a stable photoresponse over a wide spectral range, from 185 to 365 nm, with responsivity increasing monotonically with increasing photon energy. Under 365 nm illumination, the relatively low absorption coefficient of ZnO allows more photons to transmit into the hBN layer, where effective photo-dissociation of trapped carriers occurs. The device achieves a responsivity of 78.87 mA/W at 1 V bias, with an external quantum efficiency of 26.8% and a specific detectivity of 3.66×109 Jones. The rise and decay times are both 2.3 ms. In contrast, under 185 nm illumination, the strong absorption of higher-energy photons by the ZnO film suppresses the photo-dissociation process in hBN, prolongs the average carrier lifetime, and thereby markedly enhances the photoconductive gain. As a result, the device achieves a significantly higher responsivity of 2.82 A/W at 185 nm, corresponding to an external quantum efficiency of 1893.42%, a specific detectivity of 7.95 × 1011 Jones, and rise and decay times of 3.3 and 4.4 ms at 1 V bias. Moreover, the device can operate in a self-powered mode, with responsivity reaching 0.7 mA/W at 185 nm. This work presents a promising strategy for designing and applying high-performance UVA-VUV broadband photodetectors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated a p-hBN/n-ZnO heterojunction photodetector operating from 185 to 365 nm. Trap-assisted gain modulation produced responsivity up to 2.82 A/W at 185 nm, with self-powered operation also demonstrated.

articles.title_original: Wrinkling dynamics of thin crystalline sheets and its dependency on topological defects
articles.title_en: Topological Defects Shape Wrinkling in Thin Crystalline Sheets
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate the wrinkling dynamics of thin crystalline sheets under uniaxial compression using a Surface Phase-Field-Crystal-Helfrich (SPFCH) model, which captures the coupling between crystalline order, out-of-plane deformations, and topological defects. In particular, the model allows us to track and characterize two distinct classes of defects, namely those forming in the underlying hexagonal crystal lattice, such as dislocations and grain boundaries, and defects in the wrinkling patterns, known as wrinklons. By resolving the evolution and interactions of these defects, we investigate how the interplay between in-plane and out-of-plane relaxation mechanisms influences wrinkling onset and the coarsening regime. Our results indicate that crystalline defects do not affect coarsening scaling, but they quantitatively affect the onset of wrinkling and the emerging wrinkling wavelength, promote more irregular wrinkle patterns with a higher density of wrinklons, and modify long-timescale morphological evolution.
articles.summary_en: A Surface Phase-Field-Crystal-Helfrich model shows that crystalline defects alter wrinkling onset, wavelength and pattern irregularity, while leaving coarsening scaling unchanged. The findings clarify how in-plane defects and out-of-plane relaxation interact during deformation.

articles.title_original: Optical Thermometry in Monolayer WS2: Raman and Photoluminescence Spectroscopy from 5 K to 1273 K
articles.title_en: Optical Thermometry Extends Monolayer WS2 Measurements from 5 K to 1273 K
articles.excerpt_original: Reliable temperature measurement is essential for characterizing and engineering two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor devices, yet optical thermometry of 2D materials has so far been demonstrated only over narrow temperature windows spanning a few hundred kelvin. Here, we establish a comprehensive optical thermometry framework for monolayer WS2 from 5~K to 1273~K. We show that: (i) the out-of-plane A1g Raman mode shifts linearly with temperature above 100~K, with a slope of -0.0138 cm^{-1}/K in non-encapsulated WS2 (fitted over 298-1223~K) and a measurably smaller slope of -0.0121 cm^{-1}/K in an hBN-encapsulated sample (fitted over 100-1273~K); (ii) photoluminescence spectra measured over the same 5--1273~K range provide an independent optical indicator of the temperature: the neutral-exciton emission redshifts continuously with temperature and is well described by the semi-empirical Pässler model. The two indicators probe distinct physical mechanisms, lattice anharmonicity and bandgap renormalization, and together provide contact-free thermometry for monolayer WS2 from 5~K to 1273~K, an approach applicable to 2D semiconductors more broadly.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a contact-free thermometry framework for monolayer WS2 using temperature-dependent Raman shifts and photoluminescence. The approach provides independent indicators across an exceptionally broad temperature range and may support characterization of 2D semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Room-Temperature Wafer-Scale Growth of 1T′-MoTe2 for Self-Powered Broadband and Polarization-Sensitive Photodetection toward Optical Communication
articles.title_en: Room-Temperature Wafer-Scale MoTe2 Enables Self-Powered Broadband Photodetectors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The scalable integration of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors into next-generation optoelectronics demands moderate-temperature, wafer-scale synthesis routes compatible with industrial manufacturing. Here, we report the room-temperature growth of wafer-scale 1T′-MoTe2 thin films via industrial-standard RF magnetron sputtering, establishing a simple and scalable approach for high-performance optoelectronic devices. Systematic optimization of RF power, deposition pressure, and growth time enables the realization of highly crystalline 1T′-MoTe2. Raman spectroscopy confirms phase purity, high crystallinity, and polarization-dependent response, while large-area uniformity is demonstrated across a 2-inch wafer through spatial Raman mapping. The films exhibit a smooth and homogeneous morphology, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals a self-limiting surface oxide layer that passivates the film and facilitates self-powered photodetection through an intrinsic built-in electric field. Photodetectors fabricated using 1T′-MoTe2 films exhibit broadband self-powered photoresponse spanning from UV to near-infrared wavelengths (300–1550 nm), with a peak responsivity of 1.4 mA W–1 and a detectivity of 7.8 × 109 Jones at zero bias. Additionally, the devices demonstrate polarization-sensitive photoresponse with an anisotropy ratio of 2, along with imaging and optical communication capabilities, and exhibit excellent operational and ambient stability. These findings position room-temperature sputtered 1T′-MoTe2 as a promising platform for scalable, low-power, and multifunctional optoelectronic technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated wafer-scale growth of crystalline 1T′-MoTe2 at room temperature using RF magnetron sputtering, compatible with industrial manufacturing. Devices delivered broadband UV–near-infrared self-powered detection, polarization sensitivity, imaging, and optical communication capabilities.

articles.title_original: Data-Driven Framework to Accelerate Semiconductor Discovery
articles.title_en: Data-Driven Framework Accelerates Semiconductor Materials Discovery
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract This work presents a Python-based framework for the data-driven acceleration of materials discovery. It aims to autonomously identify regions of compositional space where new materials can be found, which is where more quantitatively accurate modeling techniques can focus. The software integrates an interface to materials databases, machine learning (ML) models based on the composition–property relationship, and data analysis tools. Semiconductor-specific capabilities are included, such as tailored ML feature representations. However, the framework can be applied to any material type. We discuss in detail the implemented ML models and their accuracy in predicting formation energies. These models are then validated on bismuth and lead chalcohalides, where our approach correctly identifies compositional regions where experimentally known materials absent from databases lie. As a side result, we also present thermodynamic convex hulls for Pb–S–X (X = Cl, Br, I) created by accurate atomistic simulations that are more complete than those currently available in databases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a Python-based framework combining materials databases, machine learning and data analysis to identify promising compositional regions for new semiconductor materials. Validation on bismuth and lead chalcohalides identified experimentally known materials absent from databases and produced more complete Pb–S–X thermodynamic convex hulls.

articles.title_original: Exciton diffusion dynamics with dissipation in organic molecular semiconductors
articles.title_en: New model improves exciton diffusion simulations in organic semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Exciton diffusion governs energy transport in organic molecular crystals and limits the performance of optoelectronic devices. Accurate simulation requires capturing correlated electron-nuclear motion, yet existing approaches rely on empirical treatments. Here we derive a representation-free dissipation correction for exciton dynamics from the exact factorization formalism, in which a dimensionless factor ξ quantifies dissipation through the ratio of quantum and classical nuclear momentum. Within a classical path framework, ξ is obtained from site energy fluctuations in molecular dynamics non-empirically. The exciton Hamiltonian is constructed using a semiempirical approach to describe local excitations and excitonic couplings in large systems. Applications to anthracene, perylenetetracarboxylic diimide, and quinoid merocyanine reproduce distinct exciton transport regimes ranging from localized hopping to more delocalized transport, demonstrating that an account for dissipation is essential for realistic exciton dynamics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers derived a non-empirical dissipation correction for modeling exciton dynamics in organic molecular crystals. Applications to anthracene, perylenetetracarboxylic diimide, and quinoid merocyanine reproduced transport regimes from localized hopping to delocalized motion, supporting more realistic optoelectronic-device simulations.

articles.title_original: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence Probes UV Damage in Perovskite Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Buried interfaces play a critical role in the operational stability of perovskite optoelectronic devices, yet remain challenging to probe non-destructively. Here, we demonstrate a multiwavelength photoluminescence-based approach exploiting the wavelength-dependent absorption of perovskites, enabling fast, and non-destructive probing of depth-sensitive degradation behavior of perovskite devices under operational conditions. Using ultraviolet (UV) light-soaking with different indium tin oxide (ITO) modifiers as a test case, we employ wide-field photoluminescence (PL) imaging, time-resolved photoluminescence (trPL) and ideality factor measurements with different wavelength excitation to characterize degradation behavior of both perovskite thin films and photovoltaic devices under UV soaking. Using only nondestructive characterization, we show that UV-induced degradation in p-i-n perovskite solar cells occurs preferentially at the HTL interface, adversely affecting device stability, consistent with ex-situ destructive tests. Our results also show that modifying the buried interface with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane reduces UV-induced damage at the buried interface, thus improving the UV stability of both perovskite films and devices. This work establishes a fast, non-destructive strategy to screen depth-dependent degradation in perovskite devices, offering insights for interface design and stability optimization.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a non-destructive, multiwavelength photoluminescence method for mapping depth-dependent UV degradation in perovskite films and solar cells. The study identifies the hole-transport-layer interface as a preferential damage site and finds that a 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane modifier improves UV stability.

articles.title_original: Giant Resistance Switching Ratio Exceeding 106 through a Reversible 2D–3D Structural Phase Transition in Nonequilibrium (Pb1– x Sn x )Se Thin Films
articles.title_en: PbSnSe Films Achieve Giant Resistance Switching via Reversible 2D–3D Phase Transition
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Control and switching of electrical resistance in semiconductors are important for high-performance electronic devices. Here, we realize giant resistance switching in nonequilibrium (Pb1–xSnx)Se films through a reversible structural transition between three-dimensional (3D) rock-salt (RS)-type and two-dimensional (2D) GeS-type phases. The solid-solution films were fabricated by reactive solid-phase epitaxy of SnSe/PbSe bilayers followed by rapid thermal quenching. Se-flux annealing of the PbSe template suppressed Pb precipitation, enabling chemically homogeneous, single-phase nonequilibrium RS-type films up to x = 0.58. Increasing the Sn content from x = 0.43 to 0.58 systematically increased the 2D–3D structural transition temperature and enhanced the resistance switching ratio to 4.9 × 106, far exceeding those of representative transition-metal oxide thin films (∼102–104). The giant resistance switching originates from the nearly complete transformation (∼98%) of the conductive 3D phase into the high-resistance 2D phase. These results establish crystal-dimensionality switching as a promising new mechanism for high-performance electronic switching devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a resistance-switching ratio of 4.9 × 10^6 in nonequilibrium (Pb1–xSnx)Se thin films by reversibly transforming a conductive 3D phase into a high-resistance 2D phase. The results identify crystal-dimensionality switching as a potential mechanism for high-performance semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Sustainable Thermoplastic Thermal Interface Adhesive Derived from Poly(lipoic acid) and Boron Nitride for Efficient Electronic Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Sustainable Poly(lipoic Acid)–Boron Nitride Adhesive Enables Recyclable Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The escalating power density of electronics demands thermal interface materials (TIMs) that simultaneously offer high thermal conductivity, strong adhesion, and environmental sustainability. Conventional thermally conductive adhesives (TCAs) face inherent trade-offs among these properties, often relying on non-recyclable thermosets. Here, we present a sustainable thermoplastic TCA composed of a poly(lipoic acid) (polyLA)-based dynamic polymer matrix integrated with polyvinylpyrrolidone-modified hexagonal boron nitride (BN@PVP). The polyLA matrix incorporates catechol moieties and reversible Fe3+-carboxyl/catechol coordination bonds, creating a dynamically reconfigurable network. This design yields an adhesive (LD50Fe100) with high toughness (1.52 MJ m–3), and strong lap shear adhesion (884 kPa on PMMA and 1210 kPa on steel). The dynamic bonds enable room-temperature self-healing (93.1% efficiency) and robust recyclability. At a BN@PVP loading of 40 wt %, the composite (BN@LD50Fe100) achieves a thermal conductivity of 1.2 W m–1 K–1 while maintaining enhanced mechanical properties. LED chip heat dissipation experiments demonstrate a 4 °C lower operating temperature compared to devices without a TIM, with stable thermal performance over multiple cycles. This work provides a promising material strategy to overcome the traditional trade-offs in TCAs, offering a path toward repairable, reusable, and efficient thermal management solutions for advanced electronic packaging.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a thermoplastic thermal interface adhesive combining a dynamic poly(lipoic acid) matrix with modified boron nitride. The material delivers 1.2 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ thermal conductivity, self-healing and recyclability, and reduced LED operating temperatures by 4 °C.

articles.title_original: Nanoscale mapping of native defects in Td-MoTe2 and their impact on graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures
articles.title_en: Graphene–MoTe₂ Interfaces Show Tolerance to Native Tellurium Defects
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate native defects and their impact on the electronic structure of Td-MoTe2 and graphene/Td-MoTe2 van der Waals heterostructures using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy. STM reveals a high density of circular, hollow surface defects that we attribute to Te vacancies. STS on pristine MoTe2 shows semimetallic, V-shaped dI/dV spectra with subtle low-energy states. The vacancies suppress the tunnelling conductance below the Fermi level without introducing new sharp defect-related resonances, consistent with a vacancy-induced redistribution of Mo-Te spectral weight rather than the appearance of new electronic states. In the heterostructure, graphene preserves these MoTe2 fingerprints with no noticeable graphene doping or charge transfer. Our results demonstrate that isolated native Te vacancies act as spectroscopically weak perturbations to the low-energy electronic structure of graphene. The graphene overlayer further screens their impact on the electronic structure, making graphene/Td-MoTe2 heterostructures intrinsically tolerant to such interface defects.
articles.summary_en: Scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy finds that native tellurium vacancies in Td-MoTe₂ weakly perturb the low-energy electronic structure of graphene/Td-MoTe₂ heterostructures. The graphene layer screens defect effects without noticeable doping or charge transfer, indicating inherent interface-defect tolerance relevant to van der Waals electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Generation of quantum light with tunable Wigner negativity with a semiconductor quantum dot
articles.title_en: Semiconductor Quantum Dot Generates Tunable Wigner-Negative Light
articles.excerpt_original: Wigner-negative states of light are key resources for quantum advantage in continuous-variable optical quantum computing. They can be produced probabilistically via frequency conversion and photon detection, or deterministically by exploiting the single-photon nonlinearity of a quantum emitter. Here, we generate such Wigner-negative states of light with a tunable negativity using a single semiconductor quantum dot in a cavity. Optical coherent control of the quantum-dot transition allows to generate a quantum superposition of zero and one photon. The generated quantum states are characterized point-by-point in the phase space through homodyne measurement. The emergence of Wigner-function negativity is observed as the excitation power is increased. After correcting for collection and propagation losses, we obtain fidelities to the ideal state and quantum purities above 95%, together with near-optimal quadrature squeezing. The ability to generate a wide variety of Wigner-negative states with mature semiconductor technology opens promising opportunities for continuous-variable optical quantum technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers generated tunable Wigner-negative optical states using a semiconductor quantum dot in a cavity and characterized them through homodyne measurements. The states achieved above 95% fidelity and purity after loss correction, supporting potential applications in continuous-variable optical quantum technologies.

articles.title_original: Electromotive entrainment of charge and heat currents in graphene
articles.title_en: Graphene Theory Predicts Wave-Driven Charge and Heat Currents
articles.excerpt_original: We develop a hydrodynamic theory of charge and heat currents induced by traveling waves, such as surface acoustic waves, in graphene devices near charge neutrality. The currents depend on the intrinsic conductivity and viscosity of the electron liquid, the disorder strength, and the geometry of the device. We obtain analytic expressions for the heat and charge currents to second order in the wave amplitude for Hall-bar devices. At charge neutrality and in the absence of DC bias, the heat content is entrained by the wave in the absence of net charge transfer. At the same time, device conductance is enhanced by the wave. Away from charge neutrality, the transport charge current induced by the wave arises in the absence of a DC bias.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a hydrodynamic theory showing that traveling waves can entrain heat without net charge transfer at charge neutrality in graphene devices. The model also predicts enhanced conductance and induced charge currents away from charge neutrality without a DC bias.

articles.title_original: Graphene-ITO pn junction photodetector
articles.title_en: Graphene–ITO pn Junction Photodetector Achieves 120-Fold Dark-Current Reduction
articles.excerpt_original: 본 연구에서는 플루오로벤젠을 이용한 표면 처리로 순수 그래핀 표면을 부분 불소화된 p-형 그래핀으로 기능화하였으며 p-형 그래핀 전극위에 n-형 ITO 전극을 RF 스퍼터링 방식으로 증착하여 pn 접합 기반의 광검출기를 제작하였다.
